6.2 Abstract Varieties

In order to deal with affine, quasi-affine, projective and quasi-projective varieties uniformly it is convenient to define an abstract variety. Further some constructions are more natural in this setting (for example product variety). This is analogous to the notion of manifold, and much closer to the notion of scheme. Some differences

  1. Sections of the structure sheaf are concrete 𝑘―-valued functions rather than abstract elements of a ring in the case of a scheme.
  2. When 𝑘 is not algebraically closed the underlying topological space of the corresponding scheme is the Kolmogorov Quotient (sober-ified to include all the possible generic points). When 𝑘 is algebraically closed the only difference is the inclusion of generic points.
  3. Varieties here are always Noetherian (i.e. there is a finite affine cover and the affines are themselves Noetherian).

The differences are primarily psychological and almost all the theory carries over mutatis mutandis to the scheme setting, with additional hypotheses where necessary.

Definition 6.2.1 (Abstract Variety)

A variety over a field 𝑘 is a space with functions (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) such that

  • There exists a finite open cover 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 together with isomorphisms

    𝜃𝑖:(𝑈𝑖,𝒪︀𝑋|𝑈𝑖)≅(𝑋𝑖(𝑘―),𝒪︀𝑋𝑖)

    for some affine varieties 𝑋1,…,𝑋𝑛 in the sense of (6.1.4).

The sheaf 𝒪︀𝑋 is called the structure sheaf or sheaf of regular functions. A regular morphism is then a morphism of space with functions.

It is immediate that every affine variety is an abstract variety.

Proposition 6.2.2

A variety (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) is a local space with functions. That is for all 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈), the set

𝐷(𝑓)≔{𝑥∈𝑈|𝑓(𝑥)≠0}

is open and 𝑓|𝑈 is invertible.

Proof. We have an open affine cover 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖. Then we have

𝐷(𝑓)=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖)

By (6.1.41) 𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖) is open and 𝑓|𝑈𝑖 is invertible. We deduce that 𝐷(𝑓) is open, and using the sheaf conditions that 𝑓|𝐷(𝑓) is invertible. ∎

Definition 6.2.3 (Affine (Abstract) Variety)
Let 𝑋 be a space of functions. We say it is an affine variety if it is isomorphic to (𝑌(𝑘―),𝒪︀𝑌), where 𝑌 is an affine variety in the sense of (6.1.4) and 𝒪︀𝑌 is the corresponding sheaf of regular functions (6.1.25).
Proposition 6.2.4
Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑘― be a function. Then it is regular iff the corresponding map 𝑓:𝑋→𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―) is a regular morphism of abstract varieties.

Proof. Suppose that 𝑓:𝑋→𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―) is a regular morphism. Evidently the identity map 1:𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―)→𝑘― is a regular function. Therefore by definition 𝑓:𝑋→𝑘― is a regular function.

Conversely if 𝑓:𝑋→𝑘― is regular then so is 𝑓|𝑈 for every affine open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋. By (6.1.29) and (6.1.39) this a regular morphism of abstract varieties 𝑈→𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―). By (4.3.27) we have 𝑓 is a regular morphism. ∎

6.2.1 Topological Properties

Definition 6.2.5 (Integral Variety)
We say a variety 𝑋 is integral (or irreducible) if it is irreducible as a topological space.
Proposition 6.2.6 (Criteria for Integrality)

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑋 is integral
  2. 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) is integral for every open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋
Proposition 6.2.7 (Varieties are Noetherian and Hereditarily Quasi-Compact)
Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then 𝑋 is Noetherian as a topological space and every open subset is quasi-compact (and Noetherian).
Proof. (4.1.78) and (4.1.114). ∎
Corollary 6.2.8

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then it may be expressed uniquely as a finite union of (closed) irreducible components.

𝑋=𝑋1∪…∪𝑋𝑛
Proof. See (4.1.76). ∎
Proposition 6.2.9
Suppose (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) is a space with functions such that 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 and (𝑈𝑖,𝒪︀𝑋|𝑈𝑖) is a variety. Then so is (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋).
Proof. Each 𝑈𝑖 is a finite union of affine varieties and therefore so is 𝑋. ∎
Proposition 6.2.10
Let 𝑋 be a variety. The (affine) principal open subsets form a base for the topology on 𝑋.
Proposition 6.2.11 (Varieties are Symmetric)

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then 𝑋 is symmetric as a topological space and {𝑥}― is finite for all 𝑥∈𝑋. When 𝑘 is algebraically closed then every point is closed and therefore 𝑋 is Kolmogorov.

Furthermore for every open neighbourhood 𝑈 of 𝑥 we have {𝑥}―=cl𝑈({𝑥}).

Proof. That 𝑋 is symmetric is from (4.1.44) and the affine case (6.1.18). The last statement follows from (4.1.43), then finiteness follows from the affine case. ∎
Proposition 6.2.12 (Closed Subsets of Dimension 0)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑍⊂𝑋 a closed subset. Then the following are equivalent

  1. dim𝑍=0
  2. 𝑍={𝑧1}―∪…∪{𝑧𝑛}― for some 𝑧1,…,𝑧𝑛∈𝑍
  3. 𝑍 is finite
Proof. Recall 𝑋 is Noetherian (6.2.7) and therefore by (4.1.91) we have 𝑎)⟺𝑏). Then 𝑏)⟹𝑐) is (6.2.11) and conversely if 𝑍 is finite then 𝑍=⋃𝑧∈𝑍{𝑧}― is a finite union. ∎
Definition 6.2.13 (Separated Variety)

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then we say 𝑋 is separated if for every affine variety 𝑍 and pair of morphisms 𝜙1,𝜙2:𝑍⇉𝑋 the equaliser

{𝑧∈𝑍|𝜙1(𝑧)=𝜙2(𝑧)}

is closed in 𝑍.

By (6.1.43) every affine variety is separated.

Proposition 6.2.14
Let 𝑋 be a separated variety and 𝑍 a variety. Then the equaliser of any two maps 𝜙1,𝜙2:𝑍⇉𝑋 is closed.
Proof. By definition 𝑍=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 where 𝑈𝑖 is affine. By assumption the equaliser of 𝜙1|𝑈𝑖,𝜙2|𝑈𝑖:𝑈𝑖⇉𝑋 is closed. As a finite union of closed sets is closed, we are done. ∎

6.2.2 Local Ring

We recall the definition of local ring (4.3.3) for a variety 𝑋 with irreducible subset 𝑊

𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊≔lim⟶𝑈∩𝑊≠∅𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈).

Note that if 𝑊′―=𝑊― then 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊′, so for example 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊―.

In the case 𝑊={𝑥} we write 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 for the local ring and 𝔪𝑋,𝑥 and 𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑥) for the maximal ideal and residue field respectively.

In the case 𝑋=𝑊 is irreducible then we recover the field of rational functions written 𝑘(𝑋). For a variety we can make stronger statement about the structure of 𝑘(𝑋)

Proposition 6.2.15

Let 𝑋 be an integral variety, 𝑥∈𝑋 and 𝑈 an open neighbourhood of 𝑥. Then there are canonical injections

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)↪︎𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥↪︎𝑘(𝑋)

which makes 𝑘(𝑋) the field of fractions for 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥. When 𝑈 is affine then 𝑘(𝑋) is also the field of fractions for 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈). These maps commute with the restriction maps on 𝒪︀𝑋, which are also injective.

Proof. By restricting to an affine open cover we may check that the restriction maps 𝜌𝑈𝑉 are injective. This shows that the first map is injective because every stalk can be lifted to some open neighbourhood.

Let 𝑈 be an affine open neighbourhood of 𝑥 then by (4.3.16) 𝑘(𝑋)→∼𝑘(𝑈). We may deduce from the affine case (6.1.60) that 𝑘(𝑋) is the field of fractions for 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 and 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈). ∎

As 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is isomorphic to the local ring of an affine neighbourhood we can recover many statements from the affine case.

Proposition 6.2.16

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑊⊂𝑋 an irreducible subset. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑊 is contained in only one irreducible component
  2. 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊 is an integral domain
Proof. Firstly we may reduce to the case 𝑊 is closed by considering 𝑊―. As 𝑋 is a variety, 𝑊∩𝑈≠∅ for 𝑈 affine. By (4.1.73) we may reduce to the case 𝑋 is affine, which is (6.1.61). ∎
Proposition 6.2.17 (Dominant Morphisms induce Function Field Maps)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be integral varieties and 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 a dominant regular morphism. Then there is a canonical injective 𝑘-algebra homomorphism

𝜙⋆:𝑘(𝑌)↪︎𝑘(𝑋)(𝑉,𝜎)→(𝜙−1(𝑉),𝜎∘𝜙)

This is functorial in the sense that

(𝜙∘𝜓)⋆=𝜓⋆∘𝜙⋆

If 𝜙 is an open immersion then 𝜙⋆ is an isomorphism.

Proof. See (4.3.7) and (4.3.16). ∎
Proposition 6.2.18 (Function Field Maps are compatible)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be integral varieties, 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 a dominant regular morphism and 𝑦∈{𝜙(𝑥)}―. Then for all neighbourhoods 𝑉 of 𝑦 we have a commutative diagram

In particular when identified as subrings of 𝑘(𝑋) and 𝑘(𝑌) we have the identities

𝜙⋆−1(𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥)=𝒪︀𝑌,𝜙(𝑥)

and

𝜙⋆−1(𝒪︀𝑋(𝜙−1(𝑉)))=𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉)
Proof. See (4.3.9) and (6.2.15). ∎
Lemma 6.2.19
For a variety 𝑋, 𝑅 an algebraic 𝑘-algebra and 𝜙:𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥→𝑅 a 𝑘-algebra homomorphism Then 𝜙−1(𝔪)=𝔪𝑋,𝑥 for every maximal ideal 𝔪◁𝑅.
Proof. Restatement of (6.1.62), since 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is isomorphic to local ring of affine neighbourhood. ∎
Proposition 6.2.20 (Equivalent Points)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑥,𝑦∈𝑋. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑥, 𝑦 are topologically indistinguishable
  2. 𝑥∈{𝑦}―
  3. 𝑦∈{𝑥}―
  4. {𝑥}―={𝑦}―
  5. [𝑥]=[𝑦] in the Kolmogorov Quotient 𝑋0

When 𝑋 is integral these are equivalent to 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑦 as subrings of 𝑘(𝑋).

Proof. By (6.2.11) 𝑋 is symmetric and the equivalent conditions 𝑎)-𝑒) follow from (4.1.42).

If 𝑥∼𝑦 then by definition 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑦.

Conversely suppose 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥∖𝒪︀𝑋,𝑦 in 𝑘(𝑋). In some open neighbourhood 𝑈 of 𝑥 we have 𝑓=𝑔ℎ for 𝑔,ℎ∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) and ℎ(𝑥)≠0. By definition we must have ℎ(𝑦)=0. Therefore 𝐷(ℎ) contains 𝑥 but not 𝑦, and therefore 𝑥 and 𝑦 are not topologically indistinguishable. ∎

6.2.3 Affine Varieties

We restate various results relating to “abstract” affine varieties to avoid the need to switch notations later on.

Proposition 6.2.22 (Affine Mapping Property)

Let 𝑌 be an affine variety, and 𝑋 a variety. Then there is a canonical bijection

Mor(𝑋,𝑌)⟶∼AlgHom𝑘(𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌),𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋))𝜙→𝜙𝑌♯

Proof. When 𝑋 is affine then this is just (6.1.30) and (6.1.32). In general suppose 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 is an affine covering then we have a commutative diagram

where 𝛼(𝜙)𝑖=𝜙|𝑈𝑖 and 𝛽(𝜓)𝑖=𝜌𝑋𝑈𝑖∘𝜓 and 𝛾 is the same definition as (−)♯.

By the affine case 𝛾 is bijective, and evidently 𝛼 is injective. Therefore 𝛽∘(−)♯ is injective, whence (−)♯ is injective. To show surjectivity consider 𝜓∈AlgHom𝑘(𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌),𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)) then as 𝛾 is bijective we have maps 𝜙𝑖:𝑈𝑖→𝑋 such that (𝜙𝑖)♯=𝜌𝑌𝑈𝑖∘𝜓. Suppose 𝑉⊂𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 is affine then

(𝜙𝑖|𝑉)♯=𝜌𝑈𝑖𝑉∘𝜌𝑋𝑈𝑖∘𝜓=𝜌𝑋𝑉∘𝜓

Therefore (𝜙𝑖|𝑉)♯=(𝜙𝑗|𝑉)♯ and from the affine case 𝜙𝑖|𝑉=𝜙𝑗|𝑉. As the open affines from a base (6.2.10) we conclude 𝜙𝑖|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗=𝜙𝑗|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗. Therefore there exists a morphism 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 such that 𝜙|𝑈𝑖=𝜙𝑖 and therefore 𝛽(𝜙♯)=𝛽(𝜓). Evidently 𝛽 is injective and so 𝜙♯=𝜓. ∎

Corollary 6.2.23

There is a full and faithful contravariant functor

𝐀𝐛𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐀𝐟𝐟𝐕𝐚𝐫𝑘⟶𝐑𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞𝐝𝐅𝐆𝐀𝐥𝐠𝐞𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐬𝑘

which in particular preserves and reflects isomorphisms

Let 𝑋 be an affine variety, 𝑌 a variety and 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). Then there is a canonical bijection

Mor(𝐷(𝑓),𝑌)⟶∼AlgHom𝑘(𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌),𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓)𝜙→𝜃𝑓∘𝜙𝑌♯

where 𝜃𝑓:𝒪︀𝑋(𝐷(𝑓))→∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓 is the isomorphism (6.2.21).c). The image of 𝑖:𝐷(𝑓)→𝑋 is simply the canonical localisation map.

Proof. We may apply (6.2.22). ∎
Corollary 6.2.25
Let 𝑋 be an affine variety and 𝜙,𝜓:𝑋→𝑌 regular morphisms, and 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). Then 𝜙|𝐷(𝑓)=𝜓|𝐷(𝑓) if and only if 𝜌𝑓∘𝜙♯=𝜌𝑓∘𝜓♯, where 𝜌𝑓:𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)→𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓 is the canonical localisation map.
Proof. Denote by 𝑖:𝐷(𝑓)↪︎𝑋 the inclusion then by (6.2.22) 𝜙|𝐷(𝑓)=𝜓|𝐷(𝑓)⟺𝜙∘𝑖=𝜓∘𝑖⟺𝑖♯∘𝜙♯=𝑖♯∘𝜓♯ where 𝑖♯:𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)→𝒪︀𝐷(𝑓)(𝐷(𝑓)) is simply the restriction map. We may compose this with the isomorphism (6.2.21).c) to get the required result. ∎

There are some properties of affine varieties which generalise

Proposition 6.2.26

Let 𝑋 be an affine variety and 𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑟𝐷(𝑓𝑖)
  2. (𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟)=𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)

Proof. We may reduce to the case of 𝑋 a concrete affine variety. Then

𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑟𝐷(𝑓𝑖)⟺∅=⋂𝑖=1𝑟𝑉(𝑓𝑖)=𝑉(𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟)⟺𝑘[𝑋]=𝐼𝑉(𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟)=(𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟)⟺𝑘[𝑋]=(𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟)

where we have identified 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) and 𝑘[𝑋]. ∎

Proposition 6.2.27

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). There is a canonical isomorphism

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓⟶∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝐷(𝑓))

Proof. The following is adapted from [Liu06] (Prop. 2.3.12).

Recall (6.2.2) that 𝐷(𝑓) is an open subset and 𝑓|𝐷(𝑓) is invertible. This shows that the homomorphism is well-defined, and we simply need to show it is bijective, with the case 𝑋 affine already proven (6.1.28).

Let 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 be an affine open covering then 𝐷(𝑓)=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖). By the affine case we have an isomorphism

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖)𝑓|𝑈𝑖⟶∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖))

By the sheaf conditions we have an exact sequence of 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)-modules

Localising at 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) is exact (3.6.13) and commutes with direct sums (…) so we obtain the exact sequences

where 𝛼,𝛽,𝛾 are just the canonical maps already defined. By the affine case 𝛽 is an isomorphism. We claim that diagram chasing shows 𝛼 is injective, for suppose that 𝛼(𝑥)=0 then 𝛼(𝑥)|𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖)=0 whence 𝑥|𝑈𝑖=0, and by exactness 𝑥=0. As 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 is a variety, then we conclude 𝛾 is also injective.

We further claim that 𝛼 is surjective, for given 𝑦∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝐷(𝑓)) then there exists 𝑥𝑖∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖)𝑓𝑖 such that 𝛽(𝑥𝑖)=𝑦|𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖). From injectivity of 𝛾 and exactness of the bottom sequence we conclude that 𝑥𝑖|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗=𝑥𝑗|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗, and so by exactness of the top sequence there is 𝑥∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓 such that 𝑥|𝑈𝑖=𝑥𝑖. Consequently 𝛼(𝑥)|𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖)=𝑦|𝐷(𝑓|𝑈𝑖). Exactness of the bottom sequence shows that 𝛼(𝑥)=𝑦 as required. ∎

Proposition 6.2.28

Let 𝑋 be a variety and suppose 𝑓1,…,𝑓𝑟∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) generate 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). If 𝐷(𝑓𝑖) is an affine variety for all 𝑖=1…𝑟 then so is 𝑋. Furthermore

𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝐷(𝑓𝑖)

Proof. First we claim that 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) is a reduced finitely generated 𝑘-algebra. Recall by (6.2.27) there is a 𝑘-algebra isomorphism 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓𝑖→∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝐷(𝑓𝑖)). By assumption 𝐷(𝑓𝑖) is affine so 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝑓𝑖 is finitely-generated as a 𝑘-algebra. Therefore by (3.24.21) so is 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋).

By (6.1.36) we may find an affine variety 𝑍 together with an isomorphism 𝜙♯:𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍)→∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). By (6.2.22) there is a corresponding morphism of varieties 𝜙:𝑋→𝑍, which we wish to show is an isomorphism. Let 𝑓̃𝑖≔(𝜙♯)−1(𝑓𝑖) then by definition 𝜙−1(𝐷(𝑓̃𝑖))=𝐷(𝑓𝑖).

We have a commutative diagram

whence the middle arrow is an isomorphism. As 𝐷(𝑓𝑖) is an affine variety we deduce from (6.2.23) that 𝜙|𝐷(𝑓𝑖):𝐷(𝑓𝑖)→∼𝐷(𝑓̃𝑖) is a regular isomorphism. Further 𝑋=𝜙−1(𝑍) whence the 𝐷(𝑓𝑖) cover 𝑋 and 𝜙 is a regular isomorphism as required. ∎

6.2.4 Lifting Stalk Maps

In the same way that stalks can be lifted to an open neighbourhood, for varieties we can lift stalk maps to an open neighbourhood. After reducing to the affine case this is essentially an algebraic statement about localisation.

Proposition 6.2.29 (Lifting Stalk Maps I)

Let 𝜙,𝜓:𝑋→𝑌 be regular morphisms of varieties and 𝑊⊂𝑋, 𝑍⊂𝑌 non-empty irreducible subsets. Suppose

  1. 𝑍⊂𝜙(𝑊)―=𝜓(𝑊)―, and
  2. the stalk maps 𝜙𝑊,𝜓𝑊:𝒪︀𝑌,𝑍→𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊 agree.

Then there exists an open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋 for which 𝑈∩𝑊≠∅ and 𝜙|𝑈=𝜓|𝑈.

Proof. For any open subset 𝑉′⊂𝑌 meeting 𝑍 (and therefore 𝜙(𝑊) (4.1.19)), then 𝜙−1(𝑉′) meets 𝑊. Similarly for 𝜓. So by irreducibility 𝜙−1(𝑉′)∩𝜓−1(𝑉′) meets 𝑊 (4.1.60).

Let 𝑉⊂𝑌 be an affine open subset meeting 𝑍 and choose an affine open subset 𝑈⊂𝜙−1(𝑉)∩𝜓−1(𝑉) meeting 𝑊.

From (4.3.19) we have a commutative cube for every open subset 𝑉′⊂𝑉

By uniqueness of the bottom square we conclude that (𝜙|𝑈)𝑊∩𝑈=(𝜓|𝑈)𝑊∩𝑈 and we may reduce to the case of 𝑋 and 𝑌 affine.

By (6.2.25) it is sufficient to find 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) such that 𝜌𝑓∘𝜙𝑌♯=𝜌𝑓∘𝜓𝑌♯. Suppose that 𝐷(𝑓)∩𝑊≠∅ and consider the commutative diagram

where we have used (6.2.21) to replace 𝒪︀𝑌,𝑍 with 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌)𝔐𝑌,𝑍 and 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊 with 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)𝔐𝑋,𝑊.

Let 𝑦1,…,𝑦𝑛 be generators for 𝒪︀𝑌. Then by assumption there exists 𝑡𝑖∉𝔐𝑋,𝑊 such that 𝑡𝑖𝜙♯(𝑦𝑖)=𝑡𝑖𝜓♯(𝑦𝑖). In particular 𝑓=𝑡1⋯𝑡𝑛 works, since then 𝑓𝜙♯(𝑦𝑖)=𝑓𝜓♯(𝑦𝑖) for all 𝑖. ∎

Proposition 6.2.30 (Lifting Stalk Maps II)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties, 𝑊⊂𝑋, 𝑍⊂𝑌 irreducible subsets and suppose there exists a local 𝑘-algebra homomorphism 𝜙𝑊:𝒪︀𝑌,𝑍→𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊. Then there exists an open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋 and a regular morphism 𝜙:𝑈→𝑌 such that 𝑍―=𝜙(𝑊∩𝑈)― and the following diagram commutes for all open subsets 𝑉⊂𝑌 meeting 𝑍 and 𝑈′⊂𝜙−1(𝑉) meeting 𝑊

Proof. Let 𝑌′⊂𝑌 be an open affine subset meeting 𝑍, and 𝑋′⊂𝜙−1(𝑉) an affine open subset meeting 𝑊.

Then 𝑊∩𝑋′ is an irreducible subset of 𝑋′ and similarly for 𝑍∩𝑌′ (…).

For every open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋′ meeting 𝑊 we have a commutative diagram

Therefore we may assume without loss of generality that 𝑋 and 𝑌 are affine, because we may reduce to finding a regular morphism 𝜙:𝑈→𝑌′.

We wish to find 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) and 𝜙𝑌♯ which completes the diagram

For then a regular morphism 𝜙:𝐷(𝑓)→𝑌 exists by (6.2.24). and by uniqueness (6.2.21).d) it has the required stalk map. As (6.2.19) 𝜙𝑊♯ is local we may chase the diagram to show that (𝜙♯)𝑌−1((𝔐𝑋,𝑊)𝑓)=𝔐𝑌,𝑍 and therefore 𝑍―=𝜙(𝑊∩𝐷(𝑓))― as required.

By inspection it is sufficient to find 𝑓 such that 𝑖𝑓 is injective and Im(𝜙𝑊♯∘𝑖𝑍)⊂Im(𝑖𝑓). We may find 𝑔 such that 𝑖𝑔 is injective by (3.6.37). Suppose 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌) is generated by 𝑦1,…,𝑦𝑚 then 𝜙𝑊♯(𝑦𝑖/1)=𝑥𝑖/𝑔𝑖 for some 𝑔𝑖∉𝔐𝑋,𝑊. Then 𝑓=𝑔𝑔1⋯𝑔𝑚 satisfies both criteria. As the stalk map is uniquely defined such that the diagram commutes we find that the regular morphism 𝜙 has stalk map precisely 𝜙𝑊♯. ∎

Corollary 6.2.31 (Lifting Stalk Maps I)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties, 𝑥∈𝑋 and 𝜙,𝜓:𝑋→𝑌 regular morphisms for which

  1. {𝜙(𝑥)}―={𝜓(𝑥)}―
  2. 𝜙𝑥=𝜓𝑥

Then there exists an open neighbourhood 𝑈 of 𝑥 such that 𝜙|𝑈=𝜓|𝑈.

Corollary 6.2.32 (Lifting Stalk Maps II)
Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties and 𝜙𝑥♯:𝒪︀𝑌,𝑦→𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 a local 𝑘-algebra homomorphism. Then there exists an open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋 and a regular morphism 𝜙:𝑈→𝑌 such that 𝑦∈{𝜙(𝑥)}― and has stalk map precisely 𝜙𝑥♯.

6.2.5 Open Subvarieties

Proposition 6.2.33 (Open Subset is Abstract Variety)

Let 𝑋 be a variety (resp. separated variety) and 𝑈⊂𝑋 an open subset. Then (𝑈,𝒪︀𝑋|𝑈) is a variety (resp. separated variety), which we call an open subvariety. We may write 𝒪︀𝑈≔𝒪︀𝑋|𝑈.

The inclusion 𝑖:𝑈↪︎𝑋 is an open immersion and an open immersion 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 induces an isomorphism between 𝑋 and the open subvariety 𝜙(𝑋).

Proof. By definition 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 where 𝑈𝑖 is affine. By (…) we have

𝑈∩𝑈𝑖=⋃𝛼∈𝒜︀𝑖𝐷(𝑓𝛼)

where 𝑓𝛼∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖). By (6.2.21) (𝐷(𝑓𝛼),𝒪︀𝑋|𝐷(𝑓𝛼)) is affine. Therefore we have an open cover of affine sets. By (6.2.7) 𝑈 is quasi-compact and therefore there exists a finite affine cover. This shows that 𝑈 is a variety.

Clearly the inclusion map 𝑈→𝑋 is injective and regular and so we see that 𝑈 inherits separatedness. ∎

Proposition 6.2.34 (Quasi-Affine Varieties are Abstract Varieties)

Let 𝑋 be a quasi-affine variety. Then (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) is a separated variety. More precisely there exists a full and faithful functor

𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐀𝐟𝐟𝐕𝐚𝐫𝑘⟶𝐕𝐚𝐫𝑘
Proof. This follows from (6.2.33) and (6.1.39) ∎
Proposition 6.2.35 (Morphisms into Open Subvarieties)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties and 𝑈⊂𝑌 an open subvariety. Then a regular map 𝜙:𝑋→𝑈 is regular when regarded as a map 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌.

Conversely a regular map 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 such that 𝜙(𝑋)⊂𝑈 may be regarded as a regular map 𝜙:𝑋→𝑈.

Proposition 6.2.36 (Morphisms from Open Subvarieties)
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular map of varieties and 𝑈⊂𝑋 an open subvariety. Then 𝜙|𝑈:𝑈→𝑌 is a regular map.
Proposition 6.2.37 (Patching Varieties)

Suppose 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 is a finite union of sets, (𝑈𝑖,𝒪︀𝑈𝑖) is a variety, and suppose that for all 𝑖,𝑗=1…𝑛

  • 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 is open in 𝑈𝑗, and
  • the identity map 1:(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗,𝒪︀𝑈𝑖|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)→(𝑈𝑗∩𝑈𝑖,𝒪︀𝑈𝑗|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗) is a regular morphism of spaces of functions.

Then there exists a unique structure of a variety on 𝑋 such that

  • 𝑈𝑖 is open in 𝑋, and
  • 𝒪︀𝑈𝑖=𝒪︀𝑋|𝑈𝑖.
Proposition 6.2.38 (Glueing Varieties)

Suppose 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 is a finite union of sets and there exists bijections 𝜃𝑖:𝑈𝑖→∼𝑊𝑖, with 𝑊𝑖 varieties such that for all 𝑖,𝑗=1…𝑛

  • 𝜃𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗) is open in 𝑊𝑖, and
  • 𝜃𝑖𝑗=𝜃𝑗∘𝜃𝑖−1:𝜃𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)→𝜃𝑗(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗) is regular.

Then there exists a unique structure of a variety on 𝑋 such that

  • 𝑈𝑖 is open in 𝑋, and
  • 𝜃𝑖 is a regular isomorphism.

Proof. The topology exists by (4.3.26) and we may simply define

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)≔{𝑓:𝑈→𝑘―|𝑓∘𝜃𝑖−1|𝜃𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈)regular for all𝑖=1…𝑛}

which gives 𝑋 the structure of a space of functions. As each 𝑈𝑖 is a finite union of affine varieties, so is 𝑋. ∎

6.2.6 Closed Subvarieties

Proposition 6.2.39 (Affine Closed Subvarieties)
Let (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) be an affine variety with explicit isomorphism 𝜃:𝑋≅𝑉(𝔞), and 𝑍⊂𝑋 a closed subset. Then the structure (𝑍,𝒪︀𝑍) defined in (4.3.21) is also affine with explicit isomorphism 𝜃|𝑍:𝑍≅𝑉(𝔟) where 𝔟≔𝐼(𝜃(𝑍)).
Proof. This follows largely from (6.1.44). ∎
Proposition 6.2.40 (Closed Subvariety)
Let (𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) be a variety with 𝑍 a closed subset. Then (𝑍,𝒪︀𝑍) with the structure defined in (4.3.21) is a variety.
Proof. By assumption 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 with (𝑈𝑖,𝒪︀𝑈𝑖) affine. Evidently 𝑍=⋃𝑖=1𝑛(𝑈𝑖∩𝑍) is an open cover. Further 𝑈𝑖∩𝑍 is a closed subset of 𝑈𝑖. By (6.2.39) (𝑈𝑖∩𝑍,𝒪︀𝑈𝑖|𝑈𝑖∩𝑍)=(6.2.47)(𝑈𝑖∩𝑍,𝒪︀𝑍|𝑈𝑖∩𝑍) is affine. Therefore 𝑍 is a variety. ∎
Definition 6.2.41 (Closed Immersion)
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular morphism of varieties. Then it is a closed immersion if 𝜙(𝑋) is closed in 𝑌 and 𝜙 determines an isomorphism between 𝑋 and the closed subvariety 𝜙(𝑋).
Proposition 6.2.42 (Closed Subvariety is a Variety)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑍⊂𝑋 a closed subset. Then the space with functions (𝑍,𝒪︀𝑍) is a variety and the map 𝑗:(𝑍,𝒪︀𝑍)→(𝑋,𝒪︀𝑋) is a closed immersion.

When 𝑋 is affine, then so is 𝑍 and the map 𝑗♯:𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)→𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍) is surjective.

Proof. By definition 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 where 𝑈𝑖 is affine. Then 𝑍∩𝑈𝑖 is a closed subset of 𝑈𝑖 and by (6.2.47) 𝒪︀𝑍|𝑍∩𝑈𝑖=𝒪︀𝑈𝑖|𝑍∩𝑈𝑖. Therefore by (6.2.39) 𝑍∩𝑈𝑖 is affine, and open in 𝑍. This shows that 𝑍 is a variety.

Suppose 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) then 𝑓∘𝑗∈𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍∩𝑈), which shows that 𝑗 is a regular morphism.

The final statement follows from (6.1.45). ∎

Proposition 6.2.43
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a closed immersion and 𝑌 an affine variety. Then 𝑋 is affine.
Proposition 6.2.44
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular map of varieties and 𝑍⊂𝑋 a closed subvariety. Then 𝜙|𝑍 is regular.
Proposition 6.2.45
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular map of varieties and 𝑍⊂𝑌 a closed (resp. open) subvariety. If 𝜙(𝑋)⊂𝑍 then 𝜙 may be regarded as a regular map 𝑋→𝑍.
Proposition 6.2.46
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular map of affine varieties. Then 𝜙 is a closed immersion if and only if the induced homomorphism 𝜙𝑌♯:𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌)→𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) is surjective.
Proof. Restatement of (6.1.45). ∎

6.2.7 Locally Closed Subvariety

Proposition 6.2.47 (Locally Closed Subvariety)
Let 𝑋 be a variety, 𝑍 a closed subset and 𝑈 an open subset. Then 𝑍∩𝑈 is a variety (viewed as a closed subvariety of 𝑈 or an open subvariety of 𝑍).

6.2.8 Rational Points

For abstract varieties we use a more local definition of rational point which coincides with the affine case (6.1.63).

Definition 6.2.48 (𝐾-Rational Points)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝐾/𝑘 an algebraic field extension. Define the 𝐾-rational points as follows

𝑋(𝐾)≔{(𝑥,𝜄)|𝑥∈𝑋0,𝜄:𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑥)↪︎𝐾}

where 𝑋0 is the Kolmogorov Quotient (4.1.35) of 𝑋, and recalling that 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑦 whenever 𝑥,𝑦 become equal in 𝑋0 (6.2.11).

By (6.2.19) specifying 𝜄 is completely equivalent to specifying a 𝑘-algebra homomorphism 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥→𝐾.

Proposition 6.2.49

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular morphism of varieties and 𝐾/𝑘 an algebraic field extension. Then the map

𝜙𝐾:𝑋(𝐾)⟶𝑌(𝐾)(𝑥,𝜄)→(𝜙(𝑥),𝜄∘𝜙𝑥)

is well-defined and satisfies

𝜓𝐾∘𝜙𝐾=(𝜓∘𝜙)𝐾

In particular if 𝜙 is an isomorphism then 𝜙𝐾 is a bijection.

Proposition 6.2.50 (Points = Rational Points over 𝑘―)

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then there is a canonical bijection

𝑋⟶∼𝑋(𝑘―)𝑥→([𝑥],ev𝑥)

which is functorial in 𝑋. More precisely if 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 is a regular morphism then

ev𝜙(𝑥)=ev𝑥∘𝜙―𝑥

Further

𝑦=𝜙(𝑥)⟺𝜙(𝑥)∈{𝑦}―andev𝑥∘𝜙―𝑥=ev𝑦

Proof. Recall (4.1.34) that 𝑋 may be written as a disjoint union

𝑋≔⨆𝑥∈ℐ︀{𝑥}―

for some representative subset ℐ︀⊂𝑋 which is in bijection with 𝑋0. By (6.2.11) 𝑋 is symmetric and for all 𝑧∈{𝑥}― we have [𝑧]=[𝑥] as elements of 𝑋0. So for a given 𝑥∈ℐ︀ we need to show that the map

{𝑥}―→AlgHom𝑘(𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑥),𝑘―)𝑧→ev𝑧

is bijective. It is well-defined because 𝑧∈{𝑥}― implies 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑧. Let 𝑈 be an affine open neighbourhood of 𝑥 then by (4.1.43) {𝑥}―=cl𝑈({𝑥}). Further by (4.3.15) 𝑈↪︎𝑋 induces a local isomorphism on stalks and therefore residue fields 𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑥)≅𝑘(𝔪𝑈,𝑥). By functoriality (4.3.10) we may then reduce to the case of 𝑋 affine. The result then follows from the affine case (6.1.63).

There is a commutative diagram

from which the final statement follows easily. ∎

Proposition 6.2.51

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then the evaluation map

ev𝑋:𝑋⟶AlgHom𝑘(𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋),𝑘―)𝑥→𝑓→𝑓(𝑥)

is natural in 𝑋.

When 𝑋 is affine it is also a bijection.

Proof. More precisely when 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 is a regular morphism of varieties we require to show that the following diagram commutes

Suppose 𝑔∈𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌) and 𝑥∈𝑋 then this amounts to

𝑔(𝜙(𝑥))=𝜙♯(𝑔)(𝑥)

which holds by definition.

Let 𝜃:𝑋≅𝑉(𝔞) be an isomorphism of varieties. Then 𝜙♯ is an isomorphism of 𝑘-algebras, and so −∘𝜙♯ is a bijection (since functors preserve isomorphisms). The evaluation map for 𝑉(𝔞) is a bijection (6.1.63) and so we deduce it is also for 𝑋. ∎

Corollary 6.2.52

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑈⊂𝑋 an affine open subset. Then the evaluation map

ev𝑈:𝑈⟶AlgHom𝑘(𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈),𝑘―)

is bijective.

Suppose 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 is a regular morphism, 𝑈 is an affine neighbourhood of 𝑥 and 𝑉 is an affine neighbourhood of 𝑦 such that 𝑈⊂𝜙−1(𝑉), then

𝜙(𝑥)=𝑦⟺ev𝑈(𝑥)∘𝜌𝜙−1(𝑉)𝑈∘𝜙♯=ev𝑉(𝑦)

6.2.9 Dimension

Definition 6.2.53 (Dimension of a Variety)
Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then we define the dimension to be the Krull Dimension of 𝑋 as a topological space.
Proposition 6.2.54

Let 𝑋 be an integral variety. Then it is biequidimensional and

dim𝑋=trdeg𝑘(𝑘(𝑋))

The dimension equals dim𝑈 for every open subset.

Proof. Let 𝑈 be an affine open subset then by (6.1.52) dim𝑈=trdeg𝑘(𝑘(𝑈)) which equals trdeg𝑘(𝑘(𝑋)) by (4.3.16). Further by (6.1.51) 𝑈 is biequidimensional and so by (4.1.73) we conclude that 𝑋 is biequidimensional with the same dimension as 𝑈.

Every open subset can be covered by affines so we are done by (4.1.88). ∎

Corollary 6.2.55

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then it is quasi-biequidimensional. Moreover every closed subset 𝑊⊂𝑋 satisfies the codimension formula

dim𝑋=dim𝑊+codim(𝑊,𝑋)

If 𝑊 is irreducible then we also have the identity

dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊=codim(𝑊,𝑋)=dim𝑋−dim𝑊

Proof. Every irreducible component is an integral closed subvariety and therefore biequidimensional (6.2.54). So by definition 𝑋 is quasi-biequidimensional. The codimension formula is (4.1.87).

Let 𝑈 be an affine open subset of 𝑋 meeting 𝑊. Then there is an isomorphism 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊→∼𝒪︀𝑈,𝑊∩𝑈 (4.3.17). Further by (4.1.73) we have codim(𝑊,𝑋)=codim(𝑊∩𝑈,𝑈). Therefore we may deduce from the affine case (6.1.57) that

dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊=dim𝒪︀𝑈,𝑊∩𝑈=codim(𝑊∩𝑈,𝑈)=codim(𝑊,𝑋)

as required. ∎

Proposition 6.2.56 (Irreducible Closed Subsets of Dimension 0)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑍⊂𝑋 an irreducible closed subset. Then the following are equivalent

  1. dim𝑍=0
  2. 𝑍={𝑧}― for some 𝑧∈𝑍
  3. 𝑍 is finite

In particular for every 𝑥∈𝑋 we have dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=dim𝑋.

Proof. Follows from (6.2.12). The dimension formula follows from (6.2.55). ∎
Proposition 6.2.57

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then there is a bijective correspondence

𝑋0⟷{𝑊⊂𝑍|𝑊closed and irreducible anddim𝑊=0}
Proof. By (6.2.11) and (4.1.94). ∎

6.2.10 Galois Action

The notion of rational point allows us to define a Galois Action which coincides with concrete notions in both the affine and projective cases.

Definition 6.2.58 (Abstract Galois Action)

Let 𝑋 be an abstract variety and 𝐾/𝑘 an algebraic field extension. Then there is a well-defined group action

Aut(𝐾/𝑘)×𝑋(𝐾)⟶𝑋(𝐾)

given by

𝜎,(𝑥,𝜄)⟶(𝑥,𝜎∘𝜄)

When 𝐾=𝑘― then this naturally gives a well-defined group action

Aut(𝑘―/𝑘)×𝑋⟶𝑋

in light of the bijection 𝑋→∼𝑋(𝑘―) (6.2.50).

Proposition 6.2.59 (Topological Properties of Galois Action)

Let 𝑋 be an abstract variety. For every 𝑥∈𝑋 and 𝜎∈Aut(𝑘―/𝑘) we have 𝑥 and 𝜎(𝑥) are topologically indistinguishable. Furthermore the orbit of 𝑥 is simply {𝑥}―, which has order [𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑥):𝑘].

In particular 𝜎 preserves every open set and is therefore a homeomorphism of 𝑋. Finally every 𝜎 restricts to a well-defined action on 𝑋0 which is simply the identity.

For every affine open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋 with explicit isomorphism 𝑈→∼𝑉(𝔞). Then the action of Aut(𝑘―/𝑘) coincides with the usual one under this isomorphism.

6.2.11 Product Variety

We construct the product in the category of varieties, but note that the topology of the product does not coincide with the usual product topology.

We first show that the product, if it exists, is unique in concrete sense.

Lemma 6.2.60 (Uniqueness of Product)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties (resp. affine varieties), then there is at most one topology on 𝑋×𝑌 and local space of functions 𝒪︀𝑋×𝑌 for which the projection maps are regular and the following map

Mor(𝑍,𝑋×𝑌)⟶∼Mor(𝑍,𝑋)×Mor(𝑍,𝑌)𝜙→(𝜋𝑋∘𝜙,𝜋𝑌∘𝜙)

is a well-defined bijection for all varieties (resp. affine varieties) 𝑍, natural in 𝑍.

Proof. Suppose we have two such structures, denote them by 𝑋×𝑌 and 𝑋×𝑌̃, then we have a natural bijection

Mor(𝑍,𝑋×𝑌)→Mor(𝑍,𝑋×𝑌̃)𝜙→𝜙

which is the identity on the underlying set function because 𝜙=𝜙′⟺𝜋𝑋∘𝜙=𝜋𝑋∘𝜙′and𝜋𝑌∘𝜙=𝜋𝑌∘𝜙′. By the dual version of the Yoneda Lemma (2.6.58) the identity map 1:𝑋×𝑌→𝑋×𝑌̃ is a regular isomorphism. Therefore the topology is the same and so are the sheaf of functions. ∎

Proposition 6.2.61

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties, then the categorical product 𝑋×𝑌 exists, and coincides with the set-theoretic product. More precisely

  1. there exists a unique topology on 𝑋×𝑌 and sheaf of functions 𝒪︀𝑋×𝑌 such that the projection maps 𝜋𝑋:𝑋×𝑌→𝑋 and 𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑌 are regular and there is a natural bijection for all varieties 𝑍

    Mor(𝑍,𝑋×𝑌)⟶∼Mor(𝑍,𝑋)×Mor(𝑍,𝑌)𝜙→(𝜋𝑋∘𝜙,𝜋𝑌∘𝜙)

  2. If 𝑋 and 𝑌 are affine (resp. separated), then so is 𝑋×𝑌, and there is an isomorphism

    (𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋)⊗𝑘𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌))red→∼𝒪︀𝑋×𝑌(𝑋×𝑌)
  3. If 𝑈⊂𝑋 and 𝑉⊂𝑌 are open then so is 𝑈×𝑉, and 𝒪︀𝑈×𝑉=𝒪︀𝑋×𝑌|𝑈×𝑉
  4. If 𝑇⊂𝑋 and 𝑆⊂𝑌 are closed then 𝑇×𝑆 is a closed subset of 𝑋×𝑌

Proof. Suppose 𝑋,𝑌 are both affine. Then 𝑋×𝑌 is given the structure of an affine variety in (6.1.96). This means the following map

Mor(𝑍,𝑋×𝑌)→Mor(𝑍,𝑋)×Mor(𝑍,𝑌)𝜙→(𝜋𝑋∘𝜙,𝜋𝑌∘𝜙)

is bijective when 𝑍 is affine. Consider the case 𝑍=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 is a variety. Injectivity is obvious, for surjectivity suppose 𝑓:𝑍→𝑋 and 𝑔:𝑍→𝑌 are regular. Then 𝑓|𝑈𝑖 and 𝑔|𝑈𝑖 are regular, and by the affine case so is 𝑓|𝑈𝑖×𝑔|𝑈𝑖. By (4.3.27) 𝑓×𝑔 is also regular.

Consider the general case 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 and 𝑌=⋃𝑗=1𝑚𝑉𝑗 are varieties with given affine coverings. Define 𝑊𝑖𝑗≔𝑈𝑖×𝑉𝑗, then by the affine case 𝑊𝑖𝑗 may be given the structure of an (affine) variety with regular set-theoretic projections 𝜋𝑋𝑖𝑗:𝑊𝑖𝑗→𝑈𝑖 and 𝜋𝑌𝑖𝑗:𝑊𝑖𝑗→𝑉𝑗 such that the following map is a bijection

Mor(𝑍,𝑊𝑖𝑗)→∼Mor(𝑍,𝑈𝑖)×Mor(𝑍,𝑉𝑗)

for all varieties 𝑍. Then consider 𝑍=𝑊𝑖𝑗∩𝑊𝑘𝑙=(𝜋𝑋𝑘𝑙)−1(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑘)∩(𝜋𝑌𝑘𝑙)−1(𝑉𝑗∩𝑉𝑘) regarded as an open subvariety of 𝑊𝑘𝑙. With this structure the projection maps 𝜋𝑋:𝑍→𝑈𝑖 and 𝜋𝑌:𝑍→𝑉𝑗 may be shown to be regular by

  • changing the codomain of 𝜋𝑋𝑘𝑙:𝑊𝑘𝑙→𝑈𝑘 (resp. 𝜋𝑌) to 𝑋, (6.2.35)
  • restricting the domain to 𝑍 (6.2.36),
  • changing the codomain to 𝑈𝑖 (resp. 𝑉𝑗) (6.2.35)

Consequently the identity map 𝑊𝑖𝑗∩𝑊𝑘𝑙→𝑊𝑖𝑗 is regular and therefore so is 𝑊𝑖𝑗∩𝑊𝑘𝑙→𝑊𝑖𝑗∩𝑊𝑘𝑙 (6.2.35) when considered as open subvarieties of 𝑊𝑘𝑙 and 𝑊𝑖𝑗 respectively. By symmetry this is a regular isomorphism. Therefore the 𝑊𝑖𝑗 satisfy the criteria of (6.2.37) and there exists a unique structure of a variety on 𝑋×𝑌 for which 𝒪︀𝑋×𝑌|𝑊𝑖𝑗=𝒪︀𝑊𝑖𝑗. By (…) the set-theoretic projections 𝜋𝑋:𝑋×𝑌→𝑋 and 𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑌 are regular. As before we need to show the following map is bijective

Mor(𝑍,𝑋×𝑌)→Mor(𝑍,𝑋)×Mor(𝑍,𝑌)𝜙→(𝜋𝑋∘𝜙,𝜋𝑌∘𝜙)

with injectivity obvious. Suppose 𝑓:𝑍→𝑋 and 𝑔:𝑍→𝑌 are regular. Define 𝑇𝑖𝑗≔𝑓−1(𝑈𝑖)∩𝑔−1(𝑉𝑗). Then by (6.2.36) 𝑓𝑖𝑗≔𝑓|𝑇𝑖𝑗 and 𝑔𝑖𝑗≔𝑔|𝑇𝑖𝑗 are regular. Therefore by the universal property for 𝑊𝑖𝑗 the maps 𝑓𝑖𝑗×𝑔𝑖𝑗 are regular. Clearly they are compatible so these glue to give a regular map 𝑓×𝑔:𝑍→𝑋×𝑌 (6.2.35) (4.3.27) as required. Further 𝑋×𝑌=⋃𝑖,𝑗𝑊𝑖𝑗 so it is indeed a variety. Uniqueness of the structure follows from (6.2.60).

For 𝑏) we already demonstrated that the affine product is also a product in the category of varieties, so it follows from uniqueness. For separatedness this is an easy exercise.

For 𝑐) we have 𝑈×𝑉=𝜋𝑋−1(𝑈)∩𝜋𝑌−1(𝑉) is open, and the universal property naturally restricts to the subset 𝑈×𝑉. The identity then follows from uniqueness (6.2.60).

For 𝑑) we have 𝑇×𝑆=𝜋𝑋−1(𝑇)∩𝜋𝑌−1(𝑆) is closed. ∎

Proposition 6.2.62
Let 𝑋 be an integral variety and 𝑌 a geometrically integral affine variety (see (6.1.84)). Then 𝑋×𝑌 is an integral variety.
Proof. By definition 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 for 𝑈𝑖 affine. By (6.2.61) 𝑋×𝑌=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖×𝑌 and 𝑈𝑖×𝑌 is affine. By (6.1.98) 𝑈𝑖×𝑌 is integral. By (4.1.59) 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗≠∅ whence (𝑈𝑖×𝑌)∩(𝑈𝑗×𝑌)≠∅. Therefore by (4.1.74) we conclude that 𝑋×𝑌 is integral. ∎

6.2.12 Separated Varieties

Proposition 6.2.63

Let 𝜙1,𝜙2:𝑋⇉𝑌 be regular morphisms of varieties with 𝑌 separated. Then the equaliser

{𝑥∈𝑋|𝜙1(𝑥)=𝜙2(𝑥)}

is a closed subset of 𝑋.

Proof. Let 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 where 𝑈𝑖 are affine. Then the equaliser is the finite union of

{𝑥∈𝑈𝑖|𝜙1|𝑈𝑖(𝑥)=𝜙2|𝑈𝑖(𝑥)}

which is by definition closed. ∎

The following shows that the separated property is analogous to the Hausdorff property in the classical case (4.1.98).

Proposition 6.2.64

Let 𝑋 be a variety. Then 𝑋 is separated if and only if the diagonal

Δ𝑋≔{(𝑥,𝑥)|𝑥∈𝑋}

is a closed subvariety of 𝑋×𝑋.

Proof. Suppose that Δ𝑋 is closed. Then the equaliser of 𝜙1,𝜙2:𝑍⇉𝑋 is equal to (𝜙1×𝜙2)−1(Δ𝑋). By (6.2.61) 𝜙1×𝜙2 is regular and in particular continuous. We conclude the equaliser is closed.

Conversely Δ𝑋 is the equaliser of 𝜋1,𝜋2:𝑋×𝑋⇉𝑋 and so by (6.2.14) is closed. ∎

Proposition 6.2.65
Let 𝑋 be a separated variety and 𝑍⊂𝑋 a closed (resp. open) subvariety. Then 𝑍 is separated.
Proof. Then Δ𝑍=Δ𝑋∩(𝑍×𝑍). By (6.2.61) 𝑍×𝑍 is a closed (resp. open) subvariety of 𝑋×𝑋. Then the result follows by (6.2.64). ∎
Lemma 6.2.66

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular map of varieties, with 𝑌 separated. Then the graph

Γ𝜙={(𝑥,𝜙(𝑥))|𝑥∈𝑋}

is a closed subvariety of 𝑋×𝑌. Further there is a canonical isomorphism of varieties

𝑋→∼Γ𝜙𝑥→(𝑥,𝜙(𝑥))

Proof. Consider the regular map

(𝜙∘𝜋𝑋)×𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑌×𝑌(𝑥,𝑦)→(𝜙(𝑥),𝑦)

Then

Γ𝜙=((𝜙∘𝜋𝑋)×𝜋𝑌)−1(Δ𝑌)

which is closed. The map 𝑋→Γ𝜙 is evidentally regular. Further Γ𝜙↪︎𝑋×𝑌→𝑋 is regular by (6.2.42) and (4.3.2). These are mutual inverses and so the last statement follows immediately. ∎

Proposition 6.2.67 (Intersection of Affines is Affine)

Let 𝑋 be a separated variety and 𝑈,𝑉 open subsets. Then there is a regular isomorphism followed by a closed immersion

𝑈∩𝑉⟶∼(𝑈×𝑉)∩Δ𝑋↪︎𝑈×𝑉𝑥→(𝑥,𝑥)

In particular when 𝑈,𝑉 are affine then so is 𝑈∩𝑉.

Proof. By (6.2.61) 𝑈×𝑉 is an open subvariety of 𝑋×𝑋.

(𝑈×𝑉)∩Δ𝑋=((𝑈∩𝑉)×𝑉)∩Δ𝑋 is the graph of the inclusion map 𝑈∩𝑉↪︎𝑉. By (6.2.66) it is a closed subvariety of (𝑈∩𝑉)×𝑉 and therefore of 𝑈×𝑉. The same result shows that the first map is a regular isomorphism.

When 𝑈,𝑉 are affine, so is 𝑈×𝑉. By (6.2.42) so is (𝑈×𝑉)∩Δ𝑋, and therefore 𝑈∩𝑉. ∎

Proposition 6.2.68 (Criteria for Separated Variety)
Let 𝑋 be a variety with an open cover ⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖. Then 𝑋 is separated if and only if (𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)∩Δ𝑋 is a closed subvariety of 𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗 for all 𝑖,𝑗=1…𝑛.

Proof. Suppose 𝑋 is separated then (𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)∩Δ𝑋 is a closed subvariety by (6.2.67).

Conversely if (𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)∩Δ𝑋 is closed for all 𝑖,𝑗 then by (4.1.22)

Δ𝑋=⋃𝑖,𝑗(𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)∩Δ𝑋

is closed, and therefore 𝑋 is separated by (6.2.64). ∎

Proposition 6.2.69 (Criteria for Separated Variety II)

Let 𝑋 be a variety with an affine open cover ⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖. Then 𝑋 is separated if and only if 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 is affine and the 𝑘-algebra homomorphism

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖)⊗𝑘𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑗)⟶𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)𝑓⊗𝑔⟶𝑓|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗·𝑔|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗

is surjective for all 𝑖,𝑗=1…𝑛

Proof. Suppose 𝑋 is separated, then by (6.2.67) 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 is affine and there is a closed immersion

𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗⟶∼(𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)∩Δ𝑋↪︎𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗

By (6.2.46) the corresponding map of global sections

𝒪︀𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗(𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)→𝒪︀𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)(*)𝑓→𝑢→𝑓(𝑢,𝑢)

is surjective. Recall from (6.2.61) there is a surjective 𝑘-algebra homomorphism

𝒪︀𝑈𝑖(𝑈𝑖)⊗𝑘𝒪︀𝑈𝑖(𝑈𝑗)→𝒪︀𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗(𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)𝑓⊗𝑔→𝑢→𝑓(𝑢)·𝑔(𝑢)

which composes to give the required map.

Conversely suppose that 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 are affine and the given map is surjective then evidentally the map in (∗) is surjective. By (6.2.46) this shows that the map 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗↪︎𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗 is a closed immersion and in particular (𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗)∩Δ𝑋 is a closed subvariety of (𝑈𝑖×𝑈𝑗). Then we are done by (6.2.68). ∎

6.2.13 Rational Maps

Definition 6.2.70 (Rational Maps)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties. A rational map 𝜙:𝑋⟶𝑌 is an equivalence class of regular morphisms

𝜙:𝑈→𝑌

where 𝑈 is a dense open subset of 𝑋. We say (𝑈,𝜙)∼(𝑈′,𝜙′) if there exists a dense open subset 𝑊⊂𝑈∩𝑈′ such that 𝜙|𝑊=𝜙′|𝑊.

We say the domain of definition of a rational map 𝜙 is the set of points 𝑥∈𝑋 for which there exists a neighbourhood 𝑈 of 𝑥 and a representative (𝑈,𝜙). This is a dense open subset denoted by dom(𝜙).

Proposition 6.2.71
Let 𝜙:𝑋⟶𝑌 be a rational map with 𝑌 separated. Then there exists a representative regular morphism 𝜙:dom(𝜙)→𝑌.
Proof. It is enough to show that for any two representatives (𝑈,𝜙) and (𝑈′,𝜙′) we have 𝜙|𝑈∩𝑈′=𝜙′|𝑈∩𝑈′. By (6.2.63) the equaliser is closed in 𝑈∩𝑈′ and by definition contains a dense open subset 𝑊. Therefore it equals 𝑈∩𝑈′ as required. ∎
Proposition 6.2.72 (Rational Functions are Rational Maps)

Let 𝑋 be an integral variety. Then there is a bijection

𝑘(𝑋)⟶∼{𝑓:𝑋⟶𝔸𝑘1}

and every such map is either dominant or has finite image.

Proof. By (6.2.4) this is well-defined and bijective. Suppose 𝑈⊂𝑋 is dense then by (4.1.70) it is irreducible. Therefore a regular map 𝑓:𝑈→𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―) has irreducible image (4.1.64) and 𝑓(𝑋)― is irreducible (4.1.65) and closed. Clearly dim𝑓(𝑋)―≤dim𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―)=1. If equality holds then by (4.1.83).f) 𝑓(𝑋)―=𝔸𝑘1 and by definition 𝑓 is dominant.

Otherwise dim𝑓(𝑋)―=0 whence by (6.2.56) 𝑓(𝑋)―={𝑦}― for some 𝑦∈𝔸𝑘1(𝑘―). ∎

Proposition 6.2.73

Let 𝑋 be an integral variety. Then as subrings of 𝑘(𝑋) (…) we have

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)={𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋)|𝑈⊂dom(𝑓)}

and

𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥={𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋)|𝑥∈dom(𝑓)}

Furthermore

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)=⋂𝑥∈𝑈𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥

Proof. Recall (…) that 𝔸𝑘1 being affine is separated. Therefore every rational map 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋) has a regular representative in 𝑓̃∈𝒪︀𝑋(dom(𝑓)) by (6.2.71). So if 𝑈⊂dom(𝑓) then 𝑓̃∼𝑓̃|𝑈 and so 𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈). Conversely if 𝑓̃∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) then (𝑈,𝑓̃) is a rational map whose domain contains 𝑈.

The second statement is similar, and then the final statement follows trivially. ∎

Proposition 6.2.74 (Dominant Rational Map)

Let 𝑋 be an integral variety and [(𝑈,𝜙)]:𝑋⟶𝑌 a rational map. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝜙(𝑈) is dense in 𝑌
  2. (𝑈′,𝜙′)∼(𝑈,𝜙)⟹𝜙′(𝑈′) is dense in 𝑌

In this case we say that [(𝑈,𝜙)] is a dominant rational map

Proof. Clearly 𝑏)⟹𝑎). Conversely suppose ∅≠𝑊⊂𝑈 is open, then it is dense by (4.1.59) so cl𝑈(𝑊)=𝑈 by (4.1.21). Therefore by (4.1.30)

𝜙(𝑈)=𝜙(cl𝑈(𝑊))⊂𝜙(𝑊)―

which means

𝑋=𝜙(𝑈)―⊂𝜙(𝑊)―

and therefore 𝜙(𝑊) is dense. In particular by definition we have 𝑊⊂𝑈∩𝑈′ such that 𝜙(𝑊)=𝜙′(𝑊). So we conclude that 𝜙′(𝑊) is dense and so a-fortiori is 𝜙′(𝑈′). ∎

Proposition 6.2.75

Let 𝑋,𝑌,𝑍 be integral varieties and 𝜙:𝑋⟶𝑌, 𝜓:𝑌⟶𝑍 rational maps with 𝜙 dominant. For every equivalence class (𝑈,𝜙) and (𝑉,𝜓) we have 𝑈∩𝜙−1(𝑉)≠∅ and the map

𝜓∘𝜙:𝑈∩𝜙−1(𝑉)→𝑍

is a regular morphism determining a rational map

𝜓∘𝜙:𝑋⟶𝑍

which is dominant provided 𝜓 is.

Further this is independent of the choice of equivalence class.

Proof. By definition 𝜙(𝑈) is dense which means that 𝜙(𝑈)∩𝑉≠∅⟹𝑈∩𝜙−1(𝑉)≠∅, which is therefore also dense in 𝑋 (4.1.59). ∎
Proposition 6.2.76

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be integral varieties. Then there is a bijective map

{𝜙:𝑋⟶𝑌dominant rational maps}⟶∼AlgHom𝑘(𝑘(𝑌),𝑘(𝑋))𝜙→𝜙⋆

Further 𝜙⋆ is injective and the existence of 𝜙 implies that dim𝑌≤dim𝑋. Then following are equivalent

  1. dim𝑌=dim𝑋
  2. 𝑘(𝑋)/𝜙⋆(𝑘(𝑌)) is algebraic
  3. 𝑘(𝑋)/𝜙⋆(𝑘(𝑌)) is finite

In this case we denote the degree by deg(𝜙)≔[𝑘(𝑋):𝜙⋆(𝑘(𝑌))].

Proof. The map is well-defined by (6.2.72) and (6.2.75), after we verify that the image is a 𝑘-algebra homomorphism.

Further it is injective by (6.2.29) and surjective by (6.2.30).

As 𝑘(𝑌) is a field 𝜙⋆ is injective. We claim that trdeg𝑘(𝑘(𝑌))≤trdeg𝑘(𝑘(𝑋)). For a transcendence base for 𝑘(𝑌) is a-fortiori algebraicly independent as a subset of 𝑘(𝑋). Therefore the inequality follows from (3.19.154) and (6.2.54).

𝑎)⟹𝑏) Suppose dim𝑋=dim𝑌 and let ℬ︀ be a transcendence base for 𝑌, then by (3.19.155) 𝜙⋆(ℬ︀) is a transcendence base for 𝑋. Therefore 𝑘(𝑋)/𝜙⋆(𝑘(ℬ︀)) is algebraic

𝑏)⟺𝑐) A-fortiori 𝑘(𝑋)/𝜙⋆(𝑘(𝑌)) is finitely generated. Therefore the equivalence follows from (3.19.58).

𝑏)⟹𝑎) We have a-fortiori 𝑘(𝑋)/𝜙⋆(𝑘(ℬ︀)) is algebraic whence by (3.19.154) dim𝑌≥dim𝑋, and so dim𝑌=dim𝑋. ∎

6.2.14 Tangent Space

Definition 6.2.77

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑊⊂𝑋 an irreducible subset. Define the tangent space

𝑇𝑊𝑋≔Der(𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊,𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑊))

and the cotangent space

𝑇𝑊⋆𝑋≔Hom(𝔪𝑋,𝑊/𝔪𝑋,𝑊2,𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑊))
Definition 6.2.78 (Non-Singular Point)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑊⊂𝑋 an irreducible subset. Then we say that 𝑋 is non-singular at 𝑊 if

  1. 𝑊 is contained in a unique irreducible component 𝑋𝛼 (equivalently 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊 is an integral domain), and
  2. dim𝑇𝑊𝑋=dimDer(𝑘(𝑋𝛼))

We say that 𝑋 is non-singular if it is integral and non-singular at all points.

Definition 6.2.79 (Regular Point)

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑊⊂𝑋 an irreducible subset.

We say 𝑋 is regular at 𝑊 if

  1. 𝑊 is contained in a unique irreducible component 𝑋𝛼, and
  2. dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊=dim𝑇𝑥⋆𝑋

We say that 𝑋 is regular if it is integral and regular at all points.

Proposition 6.2.80 (Regularity / Non-Singularity is a local property)

Let 𝑋 be a variety, 𝑊⊂𝑋 an irreducible subset and 𝑈⊂𝑋 an open subset such that 𝑈∩𝑊≠∅. Then there is a canonical isomorphism

𝑇𝑊𝑋→∼𝑇𝑊∩𝑈𝑈.

𝑋 is regular (resp. non-singular) at 𝑊 if and only if 𝑈 is regular (resp. non-singular) at 𝑈∩𝑊.

Proposition 6.2.81
Let 𝑋 be an integral variety. Then it is regular (resp. non-singular) if it has a regular (resp. non-singular) open cover.
Proposition 6.2.82

Let 𝑋 be a variety and 𝑊⊂𝑋 an irreducible subset such that 𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑊)/𝑘 is separably generated (e.g. 𝑘 perfect). Then there is a canonical isomorphism

𝑇𝑊𝑋⟶∼𝑇𝑊⋆𝑊

In particular when 𝑊 is contained in a unique irreducible component we have regular ⟺ non-singular.

6.2.15 Completeness

Completeness is analogous to compactness in the Hausdorff case, and many results remain true when complete is replaced with compact and the standard product topology is used (in place of the topology induced by the product variety structure). We show in the next section that every projective variety is complete, so it is quite a natural condition.

Definition 6.2.83

Let 𝑋 be a separated variety. Then it is

  • universally closed if for every variety 𝑌 the projection map

    𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑌

    is closed (i.e. the image of a closed subset is closed).

  • complete if for every irreducible closed subvariety 𝑍⊂𝑋 and valuation ring 𝑘⊂𝑅⊂𝑘(𝑍) there is a point 𝑧∈𝑍 such that 𝒪︀𝑍,𝑧⊂𝑅
Proposition 6.2.84 (Image of Complete Variety is Closed)
Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism of varieties where 𝑋 is universally closed and 𝑌 is separated. Then 𝜙(𝑋) is a closed subvariety of 𝑌.
Proof. By (6.2.66) the graph Γ𝜙 is a closed subset of 𝑋×𝑌. Then 𝜙(𝑋) is the projection of Γ𝜙 and therefore closed by definition. ∎
Proposition 6.2.85 (Closed Subvariety of Complete Variety is also Complete)
A closed subvariety of a universally closed (resp. complete) variety is universally closed (resp. complete)

Proof. Suppose 𝑍⊂𝑋 is closed then by (6.2.61) 𝑍×𝑌 is a closed subset of 𝑋×𝑌. Further 𝑇 closed in 𝑍×𝑌 implies 𝑇 closed in 𝑋×𝑌 and the result follows.

The complete case is obvious. ∎

Proposition 6.2.86
A separated variety 𝑋 is universally closed (resp. complete) iff all its irreducible components are universally closed (resp. complete).

Proof. By (4.1.66) every irreducible component is closed, and therefore complete by (6.2.85).

Conversely suppose 𝑋=𝑋1∪…∪𝑋𝑛 is the irreducible decomposition (6.2.8). If 𝑇⊂𝑋×𝑌 is closed then 𝑇∩(𝑋𝑖×𝑌) is closed in 𝑋𝑖×𝑌 and therefore by assumption 𝜋𝑌(𝑇∩(𝑋𝑖×𝑌))=𝜋𝑌(𝑇)∩𝑋𝑖 is closed. Therefore 𝜋𝑌(𝑇)=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝜋𝑌(𝑇)∩𝑋𝑖 is also closed.

The complete case is straightforward. ∎

Proposition 6.2.87

Let 𝑋 be a separated variety. To demonstrate universal closedness it is sufficient to show that

𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑌

is closed for 𝑌 affine (or even 𝑌≔𝔸𝑘𝑛).

Further it is sufficient to show that 𝜋𝑌(𝑇) is closed for all irreducible closed subsets 𝑇⊂𝑋×𝑌.

Proof. Suppose 𝑌=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖 for 𝑈𝑖 open affines. Then by (6.2.61) 𝑋×𝑈𝑖 is an open cover of 𝑋×𝑌. Let 𝑇⊂𝑋×𝑌 closed then 𝑇∩(𝑋×𝑈𝑖) is closed in 𝑋×𝑈𝑖. By assumption 𝜋𝑌(𝑇∩(𝑋×𝑈𝑖))=𝜋𝑌(𝑇)∩𝑈𝑖 is closed in 𝑈𝑖. Therefore by (4.1.22) 𝜋𝑌(𝑇) is closed in 𝑌 as required.

Clearly the closed property is preserved under isomorphism of 𝑌, therefore we may assume that 𝑌=𝑉(𝔞)⊂𝔸𝑘𝑛 is a closed subset for some 𝑛 and ideal 𝔞◁𝑘[𝑋1,…,𝑋𝑛].

By (6.2.61) 𝑋×𝑌 is a closed subset of 𝑋×𝔸𝑘𝑛. There 𝑇⊂𝑋×𝑌 is also closed in 𝑋×𝔸𝑘𝑛 and the result follows.

Finally if 𝑇 is closed then by (…) 𝑇=𝑇1∪…∪𝑇𝑚 for 𝑇𝑗 irreducible closed subsets of 𝑇 (and therefore of 𝑋×𝑌). Therefore

𝜋𝑌(𝑇)=𝜋𝑌(⋃𝑗=1𝑚𝑇𝑗)=⋃𝑗=1𝑚𝜋𝑌(𝑇𝑗)

and it suffices to show that 𝜋𝑌(𝑇𝑗) is closed. ∎

The following is not strictly needed in application to projective case as it’s already known however we include it for completeness of the argument.

Lemma 6.2.88
Let 𝑋 be an integral variety and 𝑅⊂𝑘(𝑋) is a valuation ring with local homomorphism Φ:𝑅→𝑘―. Suppose that there exists 𝑥∈𝑋 such that 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥⊂𝑅, then 𝑥 may be chosen such that Φ|𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥→𝑘― is evaluation at 𝑥.
Proof. By (6.2.19) Φ|𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is local and by (6.2.50) we may choose 𝑥′∈{𝑥}― such that Φ|𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is precisely evaluation at 𝑧′. ∎

The following proof is adapted from [Bum98] (Prop. 7.17).

Proposition 6.2.89 (Complete ⟹ Universally Closed)
A complete variety is universally closed.

Proof. We may consider the projection 𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑌 for 𝑌 irreducible affine by (6.2.87), and demonstrate that 𝜋𝑌(𝑇) is closed for every irreducible closed subset 𝑇⊂𝑋×𝑌.

Consider the closed subvariety 𝑍≔cl𝑋(𝜋𝑋(𝑇)) of 𝑋 and the irreducible and affine closed subvariety 𝑌′≔cl𝑌(𝜋𝑌(𝑇)) of 𝑌. Then evidentally 𝑇=𝑇∩(𝑍×𝑌′) and so

𝜋𝑌(𝑇)=𝜋𝑌|𝑍×𝑌′(𝑇∩(𝑍×𝑌′))

Further by (…) 𝑍×𝑌′ is a closed subvariety of 𝑋×𝑌 and 𝑇 is an irreducible closed subset of 𝑍×𝑌′. Therefore for fixed 𝑇 we may assume without loss of generality that 𝜋𝑌(𝑇) is dense in 𝑌. The composite maps

𝜋𝑌∘𝑖:𝑇↪︎𝑍×𝑌→𝑌𝜋𝑋∘𝑖:𝑇↪︎𝑍×𝑌→𝑍

are regular (6.2.42) and dominant, and we require to prove the first is surjective. Consider the injective algebra homomorphism (6.2.17)

(𝜋𝑌∘𝑖)⋆:𝑘(𝑌)↪︎𝑘(𝑇)

For any 𝑦∈𝑌 there is a corresponding evaluation homomorphism 𝜙:𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌)→𝑘― (6.2.52). By (3.25.11) there is a valuation ring (𝜋𝑌∘𝑖)⋆(𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌))⊂𝑅⊂𝑘(𝑇) and a local homomorphism Φ:𝑅→𝑘― such that Φ∘(𝜋𝑌∘𝑖)⋆ extends 𝜙.

Consider further the injective algebra homomorphism

(𝜋𝑋∘𝑖)⋆:𝑘(𝑍)↪︎𝑘(𝑇)

Then 𝑅′≔(𝜋𝑋∘𝑖)⋆−1(𝑅) is a valuation ring of 𝑘(𝑍) together with local homomorphism Φ′:𝑅′→𝑘― such that Φ′=Φ∘(𝜋𝑋∘𝑖)⋆. By hypothesis there is some 𝑧∈𝑍 such that 𝒪︀𝑍,𝑧⊂𝑅′ and by (6.2.88) we may assume that Φ′|𝒪︀𝑍,𝑧 is precisely evaluation at 𝑧.

Let 𝑈 be an open affine neighbourhood of 𝑧 in 𝑍, then by (6.2.61) 𝑈×𝑌 is an affine open subset of 𝑍×𝑌. As 𝜋𝑋(𝑇) is dense in 𝑍 then 𝑈∩𝜋𝑋(𝑇) is non-empty. This shows that 𝑈′≔(𝑈×𝑌)∩𝑇 is a non-empty open subset of 𝑇. Evidently 𝑈′ is a closed subset of 𝑈×𝑌. Therefore it is also affine (6.2.47) (6.2.42).

There is a commutative diagram (6.2.18)

By construction of 𝑅 we see that (𝑖|𝑈′)♯(𝒪︀𝑍(𝑈)⊗1)⊂𝑅 (after suitable identifications). Similarly we have a commutative diagram

and by construction we have (𝑖|𝑈′)♯(1⊗𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌))⊂𝑅 (after suitable idenitifications). By properties of the tensor product this means

(𝑖|𝑈′)♯(𝒪︀𝑍(𝑈)⊗𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌))⊂𝑅

By (6.2.42) the map (𝑖|𝑈′)♯ is surjective, therefore we conclude that 𝒪︀𝑇(𝑈′)⊂𝑅. Then by (6.2.52) the restriction of Φ to 𝒪︀𝑇(𝑈′) corresponds to a point (𝑧′,𝑦′) of 𝑈′. Further Φ∘(𝜋𝑌∘𝑖|𝑈′)♯=(Φ∘(𝜋𝑌∘𝑖)⋆)|𝒪︀𝑌(𝑌)=𝜙 and so by (6.2.52) we have (𝜋𝑌∘𝑖)(𝑧′,𝑦′)=𝑦 that is to say 𝑦′=𝑦. This shows that 𝜋𝑌∘𝑖 is surjective as required. ∎

Proposition 6.2.90

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be varieties with 𝑌 complete such that

  1. 𝑈⊂𝑋 is an irreducible open neighbourhood
  2. 𝑥∈𝑈―
  3. 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is a valuation ring
  4. 𝜙:𝑈→𝑌 is a regular morphism

Then there exists an open subset 𝑈′⊃𝑈 for which {𝑥}―⊂𝑈′ and 𝜙 lifts to 𝑈′.

Proof. We claim it’s enough to find an open neighbourhood 𝑉 of 𝑥 such that 𝑈∩𝑉≠∅ and a regular function 𝜓:𝑉→𝑌 such that 𝜓|𝑈∩𝑉=𝜙|𝑈∩𝑉. For then this extends to a regular function 𝑈∪𝑉 as required.

Replacing 𝑋=𝑈― we may assume that 𝑈 is dense in 𝑋 and 𝑋 is irreducible. Observe 𝑍≔cl𝑌(𝜙(𝑈)) is an irreducible closed subset of 𝑌 (4.1.70) (4.1.65). Therefore there is an injective 𝑘-algebra homomorphism (4.3.16)

𝜙⋆:𝑘(𝑍)↪︎𝑘(𝑈)⟶∼𝑘(𝑋)

By assumption 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is a valuation ring, whence so is the inverse image 𝑅. By assumption there is 𝑧∈𝑍 such that 𝒪︀𝑍,𝑧⊂𝑅. Therefore we have a 𝑘-algebra homomorphism 𝒪︀𝑍,𝑧→𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥. By (6.2.32) this lifts to a regular morphism 𝜓:𝑉→𝑍⊂𝑌 for which 𝑥∈𝑉. As 𝑥∈𝑈― we have 𝑈∩𝑉≠∅ by (4.1.19). As 𝑌 is separated (6.2.63) the equaliser of 𝜙,𝜓 is a closed subset of 𝑈∩𝑉. We have by construction a commutative diagram

Regarding 𝜓:𝑋⟶𝑌 as a rational map we find by (6.2.76) that 𝜓⋆=𝜙⋆ whence 𝜓=𝜙 as rational maps. This means that the equaliser contains a dense open subset of 𝑈∩𝑉 and being closed is therefore the whole set. That is 𝜙|𝑈∩𝑉=𝜓|𝑈∩𝑉 as required. ∎

6.2.16 Projective Space

We introduce the notion of projective varieties by showing that projective space can naturally be given the structure of an abstract variety. A more low-tech approach is taken in the Projective Varieties section, where the constructions are shown to be equivalent.

Definition 6.2.91 (Projective Space)

Let 𝐾 be a field extension define

ℙ𝑛(𝐾)≔𝐾𝑛+1∖{(0,…,0)}/∼

where

(𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑛)∼(𝑥0′,…,𝑥𝑛′)⟺𝑥𝑖=𝜆𝑥𝑖′some𝜆∈𝐾⋆

and write (𝑥0:…:𝑥𝑛) for the corresponding equivalence class in ℙ𝑛(𝐾).

Lemma 6.2.92 (Comparing projective points)

Consider two projective points 𝑥=(𝑥0:…:𝑥𝑛) and 𝑦=(𝑦0:…:𝑦𝑛).

  1. 𝑥=𝑦⟹∀𝑖(𝑥𝑖=0⟺𝑦𝑖=0)

Suppose that 𝑥𝑖≠0 for some 𝑖. Then 𝑥=𝑦 iff

  1. 𝑦𝑖≠0
  2. 𝑥𝑗𝑥𝑖=𝑦𝑗𝑦𝑖 for all 𝑗
Proposition 6.2.93 (Projective Space)

Consider the set 𝑋=ℙ𝑛(𝑘―) and for every 𝑖=0,…,𝑛 define the subset

𝑈𝑖≔{(𝑥0:…:𝑥𝑛)|𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑛∈𝑘―,𝑥𝑖≠0}.

There are canonical bijections

𝜃𝑖:𝑈𝑖⟶∼𝔸𝑘𝑛(𝑘―)𝑖=0…𝑛(𝑥0:…:𝑥𝑛)→(𝑥0𝑥𝑖,…,𝑥𝑖𝑥𝑖̂,…,𝑥𝑛𝑥𝑖)(𝑧1:…:1:…:𝑧𝑛)←(𝑧1,…,𝑧𝑛)

and there is a unique topology on 𝑋 and space of functions 𝒪︀𝑋 such that 𝑈𝑖 is open in 𝑋 and 𝜃𝑖 is a regular isomorphism for all 𝑖=0…𝑛.

Denote this by ℙ𝑘𝑛. With this structure ℙ𝑘𝑛 is an irreducible, separated algebraic variety of dimension 𝑛.

Further for any homogenous polynomial 𝐹∈𝑘[𝑋0,…,𝑋𝑛] of degree 𝑑 the expression

(𝑥0:…:𝑥𝑛)→𝐹(𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑛)𝑥𝑖𝑑

is a well-defined regular function on 𝑈𝑖. In particular on 𝑈𝑖 we may define the homogenous coordinate functions 𝑋0𝑋𝑖,…,𝑋𝑛𝑋𝑖.

Proof. It is straightforward to show that 𝜃𝑖 is a bijection. Define the cocycle maps

𝜃𝑖𝑗:𝜃𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)→𝜃𝑗(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)

by 𝜃𝑖𝑗=𝜃𝑗∘𝜃𝑖−1. We show that 𝜃𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗) is open in 𝔸𝑘𝑛(𝑘―) and the maps 𝜃𝑖𝑗 are regular. First observe that

𝜃𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)={𝐷(𝑍𝑗)𝑖<𝑗𝐷(𝑍𝑗+1)𝑗<𝑖

Then the cocycle map is given pointwise by

𝜃𝑖𝑗:𝐷(𝑍𝑗)→𝐷(𝑍𝑖+1)(𝑧1,…,𝑧𝑛)→(𝑧1𝑧𝑗,…,𝑧𝑖𝑧𝑗,1𝑧𝑗,…,𝑧𝑛𝑧𝑗)

Using (6.2.45) and (6.1.39) we may show that 𝜃𝑖𝑗 is a regular morphism of abstract varieties. Therefore the structure on 𝑋 is uniquely determined by (6.2.38).

By construction 𝑈𝑖 is affine and 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗=𝐷(𝑋𝑗𝑋𝑖) where 𝑋𝑗𝑋𝑖∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖). Therefore 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 is affine by (6.2.21) and there is a canonical isomorphism

𝒪︀𝑈𝑖(𝑈𝑖)𝑋𝑗𝑋𝑖⟶∼𝒪︀𝑈𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)

As 𝑋𝑖𝑋𝑗∈𝒪︀𝑈𝑗(𝑈𝑗) satisfies 𝑋𝑖𝑋𝑗|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗=(𝑋𝑗𝑋𝑖|𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)−1 we find the canonical map

𝒪︀𝑈𝑖(𝑈𝑖)⊗𝒪︀𝑈𝑗(𝑈𝑗)→𝒪︀𝑈𝑖(𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗)

is surjective. Therefore 𝑋 is separated by (6.2.69).

By (6.1.21) the affine space 𝔸𝑘𝑛 is irreducible whence so is 𝑈𝑖 and 𝑈𝑖∩𝑈𝑗 (4.1.70). Therefore by (4.1.74) ℙ𝑘𝑛 is irreducible and has dimension 𝑛 by (4.1.88). ∎

Proposition 6.2.94 (Riemann Sphere)

There is a bijection

ℙ𝑘1⟶∼𝔸𝑘1∪{∞}

which sends (𝑥:1) to 𝑥 and (1:0) to ∞. This gives 𝔸𝑘1∪{∞} the structure of a variety under which 𝔸𝑘1 is an open subvariety and 𝑥−1 is a regular automorphism interchanging 0 and ∞.

Consider 𝑥=𝑋1𝑋0∈𝒪︀ℙ𝑘1(𝑈0) as an element of the function field 𝑘(ℙ𝑘1) then 𝑥 is transcendental and 𝑘(ℙ𝑘1)=𝑘(𝑥).

Proof. Evidently 𝑥 is transcendental because 𝒪︀(𝑈0)=𝑘[𝑥] (…). Let 𝑓∈𝑘(ℙ𝑘1) and suppose dom(𝑓)∩𝑈0≠∅. There is some 𝑔(𝑥)∈𝒪︀(𝑈0) such that 𝐷(𝑔(𝑥))⊂dom(𝑓). Then by (…) 𝒪︀(𝐷(𝑔))=𝑘[𝑥]𝑔(𝑥) and so 𝑓|𝐷(𝑔(𝑥))=ℎ(𝑥)/𝑔(𝑥)𝑟 for some polynomial ℎ∈𝑘[𝑋] and integer 𝑟>0. Therefore 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑥). Similarly if dom(𝑓)∩𝑈1≠∅ then 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑥−1)=𝑘(𝑥) as required, where 𝑥−1=𝑋0𝑋1∈𝒪︀ℙ𝑘1(𝑈1). ∎

We show later that all projective closed subvarieties are complete, but here we demonstrate a simpler case more directly.

Proposition 6.2.95
ℙ𝑘1 is complete.
Proof. Let 𝑍⊂ℙ𝑘1 be an irreducible closed subvariety. Then by (4.1.83) (6.2.56) it is either the (closure of) a single point or the whole space. In the former case the function field is algebraic over 𝑘 and has no non-trivial valuation rings. Therefore we may assume wlog that 𝑍=ℙ𝑘1 and consider a valuation ring 𝑅⊂𝑘(ℙ𝑘1)=𝑘(𝑥) where 𝑥=𝑋1𝑋0. By (3.37.8) 𝑅 is equal to either 𝑘[𝑥]𝑝(𝑥) for some irreducible polynomial or 𝑘[𝑥−1]𝑥−1. Let 𝛼 be a root of 𝑝(𝑥) in 𝑘―, then this corresponds to the point (1:𝛼), or in the latter case just (0:1). ∎

6.2.17 Affine and Finite Morphisms

Definition 6.2.96

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular morphism of varieties. We say 𝜙 is affine if for every affine open 𝑉⊂𝑌, 𝜙−1(𝑉) is affine.

We say in addition that 𝜙 is finite if the ring map 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉)→𝒪︀𝑋(𝜙−1(𝑉)) is finite (and therefore integral …).

Other than the definition we do not require this section in the sequel. But it may be convenient for other applications to show that it’s sufficient to demonstrate a morphism is affine (resp. finite) only over a single affine cover.

Lemma 6.2.97

Let 𝑋 be a variety with 𝑈,𝑉 open affine subsets. Then there exists 𝑔1,…,𝑔𝑟∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) and 𝑔1′,…,𝑔𝑟′∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑉) such that

  1. 𝑊𝑖≔𝐷(𝑔𝑖)=𝐷(𝑔𝑖′) for 𝑖=1…𝑟
  2. 𝑈∩𝑉=⋃𝑖=1𝑟𝑊𝑖
Proof. Given 𝑥∈𝑈∩𝑉, then as 𝑈∩𝑉 is open in 𝑈 by (6.2.10) we may find 𝑓𝑥∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) such that 𝑥∈𝐷(𝑓𝑥)⊂𝑈∩𝑉. Similarly we may find 𝑓𝑥′∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑉) with 𝑥∈𝐷(𝑓𝑥′)⊂𝐷(𝑓𝑥). By (6.2.21).c) there is a canonical isomorphism 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)𝑓𝑥→∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝐷(𝑓𝑥)). Therefore 𝑓𝑥′|𝐷(𝑓𝑥)=𝑔(𝑓𝑥)𝑟 for some 𝑔∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈). Observe that 𝐷(𝑓𝑥′)=𝐷(𝑔)∩𝐷(𝑓𝑥)=𝐷(𝑔𝑓𝑥). This gives the required pair of sections for an arbitrary 𝑥∈𝑈∩𝑉. Clearly these open sets cover 𝑈∩𝑉, and as 𝑈∩𝑉 is quasi-compact (6.2.7) we are done. ∎
Proposition 6.2.98

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular morphism of varieties, and suppose there is an open cover 𝑌=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑉𝑖 for which 𝑉𝑖 and 𝜙−1(𝑉𝑖) are affine. Then 𝜙 is affine.

If in addition 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉𝑖)→𝒪︀𝑋(𝜙−1(𝑉𝑖)) is finite for all 𝑖=1…𝑛 then 𝜙 is finite.

Proof. By assumption we have affine open sets 𝑈𝑖≔𝜙−1(𝑉𝑖) for 𝑖=1…𝑛. Let 𝑉⊂𝑌 be an open affine set, then by (6.2.97) for each 𝑖 we have an open cover

𝑉∩𝑉𝑖=⋃𝑗=1𝑛𝑖𝑊𝑖𝑗

with 𝑊𝑖𝑗≔𝐷(𝑓𝑖𝑗)=𝐷(𝑓𝑖𝑗′) for 𝑓𝑖𝑗′∈𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉𝑖) and 𝑓𝑖𝑗∈𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉). Evidently

𝑉=⋃𝑖=1𝑛⋃𝑗=1𝑛𝑖𝐷(𝑓𝑖𝑗)(*)

and so by (6.2.26) the 𝑓𝑖𝑗 generate 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉), and consequentally 𝑔𝑖𝑗≔𝜙♯(𝑓𝑖𝑗) generate 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) (as both ideals contain 1). Further 𝜙−1(𝑊𝑖𝑗)=𝜙−1(𝐷(𝑓𝑖𝑗′))=𝐷(𝜙♯(𝑓𝑖𝑗′))⊂𝑈𝑖 is affine (6.2.21).c). Therefore from (6.2.28) 𝑈 is affine, because we also have the representation 𝜙−1(𝑊𝑖𝑗)=𝜙−1(𝐷(𝑓𝑖𝑗))=𝐷(𝑔𝑖𝑗).

Suppose 𝜙 is finite then by definition this means the ring maps 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉𝑖)→𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈𝑖) are finite. By (3.6.48).a) this means the localised maps are finite

Using equation (∗) and (6.2.26) we see that 𝑓𝑖𝑗 generate the unit ideal of 𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉). Therefore by (3.6.48).b) 𝜙𝑉♯ is finite. ∎

6.2.18 Normal Varieties

Definition 6.2.99

Let 𝐴 be an integral domain. We say that the ring 𝐴 is normal if it is integrally closed in its field of fractions.

Recall that 𝐴 factorial ⟹ 𝐴 is normal (3.24.12).

Proposition 6.2.100
The polynomial ring 𝐴[𝑋1,…,𝑋𝑛] is normal for every unique factorisation domain 𝐴.
Proof. See (3.24.12) and (3.17.35). ∎
Proposition 6.2.101 (Normal Variety)

Let 𝑋 be an integral variety. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) is normal for every open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋
  2. 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊 is normal for every irreducible subset 𝑊⊂𝑋
  3. 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is normal for every point 𝑥∈𝑋

In this case we say that 𝑋 is a normal variety. If 𝑋 is affine then this is equivalent to 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋) being normal.

Proof. 𝑎)⟹𝑏) Let 𝑈⊂𝑋 be any affine open subset such that 𝑈∩𝑊≠∅, then by (…) 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑊→∼𝒪︀𝑈,𝑊∩𝑈→∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)𝔐𝑈,𝑊∩𝑈, and the result follows from (3.24.10).

𝑏)⟹𝑐) is straightforward because 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=𝒪︀𝑋,{𝑥}.

𝑐)⟹𝑎) We first show this for the case that 𝑈 is affine. By (…) 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥→∼𝒪︀𝑈,𝑥→∼𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)𝔐𝑈,𝑥 is normal for every 𝑥∈𝑈. Therefore by (6.2.21).b) and (3.24.10) 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) is normal.

Now let 𝑈 be an arbitrary open set and 𝑉⊂𝑈 affine. Then by (6.2.15) we have inclusions

𝒪︀𝑋(𝑉)↪︎𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)↪︎Frac(𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈))↪︎𝑘(𝑋)

and 𝑘(𝑋) is a fraction field for 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑉). If 𝛼∈Frac(𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)) is integral over 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈), then it is a-fortiori integral over 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑉). By the affine case then 𝛼∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑉) and we conclude that 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) is normal as required.

For the case 𝑋 is affine we may use (3.24.10). ∎

Corollary 6.2.102
The standard affine space 𝔸𝑘𝑛(𝑘―) is normal.
Proof. The coordinate ring is a UFD (3.17.35) and therefore normal (3.24.12). ∎
Proposition 6.2.103
Let 𝑋 be an integral variety with open cover 𝑋=⋃𝑖=1𝑛𝑈𝑖. Then 𝑋 is normal iff 𝑈𝑖 are normal.
Proof. Straightforward, since normality is a local condition. ∎

6.2.19 Weil Divisors

The notion of regular curves can be generalised in one direction.

Definition 6.2.104 (Prime Divisors of an Integral Variety)

Let 𝑋 be an integral, separated variety. We say it is regular in codimension one if for every irreducible closed subset 𝑌⊂𝑋 for which codim(𝑌,𝑋)=1 the local ring 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑌 is regular (equivalently integrally closed or a DVR (3.31.2)).

In this case, we say an irreducible closed subset of codimension 1 is a prime divisor.

We denote by Div𝑋 the free abelian group generated by the prime divisors. We write a prime divisor 𝐷 by a formal sum

𝐷=∑𝑌⊂𝑋𝑛𝑌𝑌

where 𝑛𝑌∈ℤ and all but finitely many are zero. We define the degree of a divisor 𝐷 by

deg𝐷=∑𝑌⊂𝑋𝑛𝑌[𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑌):𝑘]
Proposition 6.2.105

An integral, separated variety 𝑋 is regular in codimension one for either of the following special cases

  1. 𝑋 is normal
  2. 𝑋 is non-singular and 𝑘 is perfect.
Proof. See (3.31.2) and (6.2.82). ∎
Proposition 6.2.106 (Valuation Associated to Prime Divisor)

Let 𝑋 be a variety satisfying (6.2.104) and 𝑌⊂𝑋 a prime divisor. Then 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑌 is a discrete valuation ring.

We denote by 𝑣𝑌:𝑘(𝑋)⋆→ℤ the corresponding valuation.

Proof. By (6.2.55) dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑌=codim(𝑌,𝑋)=1 and is integral, so the result follows from (3.31.2). ∎
Proposition 6.2.107 (Prime Divisors on a Curve)
Let 𝑋 be a regular curve. Then 𝑋 satisfies (6.2.104) and the prime divisors are precisely irreducible closed subsets of the form {𝑥}―. These are in bijective correspondence with the valuation rings of 𝑘(𝑋), via the map 𝑥→𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥.
Proof. By the codimension formula (6.2.55) the irreducible closed subsets of codimension 1 are precisely those of dimension 0. Therefore the result follows from (6.2.114). ∎
Proposition 6.2.108
Let 𝑋 be a variety satisfying (6.2.104) and 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋)⋆ a rational function. Then 𝑣𝑌(𝑓)=0 for all but finitely many prime divisors 𝑌.

Proof. By definition 𝑓 is regular on some open subset 𝑈 of 𝑋, which we may assume to be affine. Define 𝑍≔𝑋∖𝑈. Then by (…) 𝑍=𝑍1∪…∪𝑍𝑛 is a decomposition into irreducible components. By (4.1.83).f) codim(𝑍,𝑋)>0 whence codim(𝑍𝑖,𝑋)>0 for all 𝑖=1…𝑛. Suppose 𝑌⊂𝑍 is a prime divisor then by definition codim(𝑌,𝑋)=1 and by (4.1.66) 𝑌⊂𝑍𝑖 for some 𝑖. Therefore by (4.1.83).c) codim(𝑌,𝑍𝑖)≤codim(𝑌,𝑋)−codim(𝑍𝑖,𝑋)≤0 and therefore by (4.1.83).f) 𝑌=𝑍𝑖.

We conclude all but finitely many 𝑌 intersect 𝑈, so we may without loss of generality assume 𝑌∩𝑈≠∅. Evidently 𝑈 also satisfies (6.2.104) and by (4.1.79) there is a bijection between prime divisors of 𝑋 meeting 𝑈, and prime divisors of 𝑈.

Therefore we may assume that 𝑋 is affine and 0≠𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋(𝑋). Then 𝑣𝑌(𝑓)>0⟺𝑓∈𝔐𝑋,𝑌⟺𝑓∈𝐼(𝑌)⟺𝑌⊂𝑉(𝑓). We claim 𝑉(𝑓) is a proper subset of 𝑋 (for 𝑉(𝑓)=𝑋⟺(0)=𝑓⟺𝑓=0). Therefore codim(𝑉(𝑓),𝑋)>0 and

codim(𝑌,𝑉(𝑓))≤codim(𝑌,𝑋)−codim(𝑉(𝑓),𝑋)≤0

so 𝑌 is an irreducible component of 𝑉(𝑓), of which there are only finitely many (4.1.66). ∎

Definition 6.2.109 (Principal Divisor)

Let 𝑋 be a variety satisfying (6.2.104) then define the homomorphism

𝑘(𝑋)⋆⟶Div(𝑋)𝑓⟶(𝑓)

where we define a formal sum over all prime divisors

(𝑓)≔∑𝑌⊂𝑋𝑣𝑌(𝑓)𝑌.

The co-kernel of this map is known as the divisor class group of 𝑋, and denoted Cl(𝑋). We say that two divisors are equivalent 𝐷∼𝐷′ if they become equal as elements of the divisor class group. Equivalently if 𝐷−𝐷′=(𝑓) for some 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋)⋆.

6.2.20 Algebraic Curves

Definition 6.2.110
We say an integral, separated algebraic variety of dimension 1 is an algebraic curve or just a curve.
Proposition 6.2.111 (Characterisation Regular Point on a curve)

Let 𝑋 be an algebraic curve and 𝑥∈𝑋. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑥 is regular
  2. 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is a discrete valuation ring
  3. 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is an integrally closed domain

and when 𝑘 is perfect this is equivalent to 𝑥 being non-singular.

In particular 𝑋 is regular if and only if it is normal.

Proof. Follows exactly the same lines as (6.1.100). ∎
Example 6.2.112
Both 𝔸𝑘1 and ℙ𝑘1 are regular algebraic curves.
Proposition 6.2.113 (Curve has Cofinite Topology)
Let 𝑋 be an algebraic curve (or just an algebraic variety of dimension 1) then 𝑋0 has the cofinite topology.
Proof. Follows from (4.1.92). ∎
Proposition 6.2.114 (Points on Complete Regular Curve = Valuation Rings on Function Field)

Let 𝑋 be a complete regular algebraic curve. Then there is a bijection

{𝑊⊂𝑋|dim𝑊=0closed and irreducible}⟷𝑋0⟷{𝑘⊂𝑅⊊𝑘(𝑋)|𝑅a valuation ring}

Further the corresponding valuation rings are all discrete valuation rings.

For an affine open subset 𝑈⊂𝑋 this restricts to a bijection

𝑈0⟷{𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)⊂𝑅⊊𝑘(𝑋)|𝑅a valuation ring}

where 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) is identified as a subring of 𝑘(𝑋) (6.2.18).

Proof. The first map is (4.1.94) and the second map is well-defined by (6.2.111) and injective by (6.2.20).

Let 𝑅⊂𝑘(𝑋) be a valuation ring then by definition of completeness there is a point 𝑥∈𝑋 such that 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥⊂𝑅. By (6.2.55) we have dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥=dim𝑋=1. By (6.1.92) and (6.1.91) 1=dim𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥≤dim𝑅≤trdeg𝑘𝑘(𝑋)=(6.2.54)dim𝑋=1. Therefore dim𝑅=1 and by the same result 𝑅=𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥. This shows that the map is surjective.

For the final statement we may use the affine case (6.1.101) and the commutative diagram

 ∎

Proposition 6.2.115

Let 𝑋 be a regular algebraic curve and 𝑌 a complete variety. Then the rational maps are precisely the regular maps. In otherwords the canonical map

Mor(𝑋,𝑌)⟶∼Rat(𝑋,𝑌)

is a bijection. Further this restricts to dominant maps.

Proof. Clearly the map is well-defined. Suppose that two regular maps 𝜙,𝜓 are equal as rational maps. Then by definition they agree on a dense open subset. By definition 𝑌 is separated so by (6.2.63) the equaliser is a closed subset, and therefore the whole of 𝑌. This means the map is injective.

Consider a regular map 𝜙:𝑈→𝑌 for 𝑈 a (dense) open subset of 𝑋. Then 𝑍≔𝑋∖𝑈 is a proper closed subset of 𝑋 and therefore dim𝑍=0 by (4.1.84). By (6.2.12) we have 𝑍={𝑧1}―∪…∪{𝑧𝑛}―, and we may apply (6.2.90) finitely many times to lift to a regular map on an open set containing 𝑈 and 𝑧1,…,𝑧𝑛. By (4.1.41) this is the whole of 𝑋. Therefore the given map is surjective. ∎

Proposition 6.2.116 (Image of Complete Curve either Constant or Surjective)
Let 𝑋,𝑌 be algebraic curves with 𝑋 complete and 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 a regular morphism. Then 𝜙 is either surjective or has image of the form {𝑥}― (which we call constant).
Proof. By (6.2.89) 𝜙 is universally closed, so by (6.2.84) 𝜙(𝑋) is an irreducible closed subvariety of 𝑌. Evidently dim𝜙(𝑋)=0 or 1. Then we may use (6.2.56) or (4.1.84). ∎
Corollary 6.2.117 (Equivalence between nice curves and function fields)

Let 𝑋,𝑌 be complete, regular algebraic curves. Then there are bijections

{𝜙:𝑋→𝑌non-constant}⟷{𝜙:𝑋⟶𝑌dominant}⟷{𝜙⋆:𝑘(𝑌)↪︎𝑘(𝑋)}

All such morphisms are surjective and the degree

deg(𝜙)≔[𝑘(𝑋):𝜙⋆(𝑘(𝑌))]

is always finite.

Finally the fibres are finite (i.e. 𝜙 is “quasi-finite”).

Proof. This follows from (6.2.116), (6.2.115) and (6.2.76).

The fibres are finite because 𝜙−1({𝑦})⊂𝜙−1({𝑦}―). By assumption this is a proper closed subset of 𝑋 and therefore has dimension 0. So we are done by (6.2.56). ∎

Proposition 6.2.118

Let 𝑋 be a regular algebraic curve. Then there is a bijection

𝑘(𝑋)⋆⟷{𝜙:𝑋→ℙ𝑘1non-constant}

More precisely given 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋)⋆, then for 𝑥∈𝑋 the function

𝜙𝑓(𝑥)={(𝑓(𝑥):1)𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥(1:𝑓−1(𝑥))𝑓−1∈𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥

is well-defined and regular.

Proof. Recall (6.2.111) (6.2.15) that 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is a (discrete) valuation ring with field of fractions 𝑘(𝑋).

Define the open subsets 𝑈≔dom(𝑓) and 𝑉≔dom(𝑓−1). We claim that 𝑋=𝑈∪𝑉. For 𝑥∈dom(𝑓)⟺𝑓∈𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 and as 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is a valuation ring for 𝑘(𝑋) then we have either 𝑥∈𝑈 or 𝑥∈𝑉.

Define 𝜙:𝑈→ℙ𝑘1 by 𝜙(𝑥)=(𝑓(𝑥):1), and similarly 𝜓:𝑉→ℙ𝑘1 by 𝜓(𝑥)=(1:𝑓−1(𝑥)). By definition of projective structure sheaf (6.2.93) these are regular. Then for 𝑥∈𝑈∩𝑉 we must have 𝑓∉𝔪𝑋,𝑥 that is 𝑓(𝑥)≠0 and 𝑓−1(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑥)−1. This shows that 𝜙|𝑈∩𝑉=𝜓|𝑈∩𝑉. Therefore they glue to a well-defined regular map 𝑋→ℙ𝑘1 as required.

We note that 𝜙𝑓−1(𝑈1)=dom(𝑓) where 𝑈1 is the second affine piece, and we conclude the map is injective.

Conversely given a morphism 𝜙:𝑋→ℙ𝑘1 then 𝑈≔𝜙−1(𝑈1) is a non-empty open subset of 𝑋 and 𝑓:𝑋0/𝑋1∘𝜙|𝑈:𝑈→𝑘― is a regular function. Evidently 𝜙|𝑈=𝜙𝑓|𝑈, and we conclude 𝜙=𝜙𝑓 by (6.2.115). Therefore the map is surjective. ∎

Proposition 6.2.119 (Regular Morphisms of Complete Curves are Finite)

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a non-constant morphism of complete regular algebraic curves. Suppose 𝑉⊂𝑌 is an affine open subset, then

𝒪︀𝑋(𝜙−1(𝑉))=𝜙⋆(𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉))―

where ⋅― denotes the integral closure in 𝑘(𝑋).

Further 𝜙 is a finite (and therefore affine, and integral) morphism.

Proof. Define 𝐴≔𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉) and 𝐵≔𝜙⋆(𝐴)―. Then

𝐵=⋂𝜙⋆(𝐴)⊂𝑅𝑅(3.25.14)
=⋂𝐴⊂𝜙⋆−1(𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥)𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥(6.2.114)
=⋂𝐴⊂𝒪︀𝑌,𝜙(𝑥)𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥(6.2.18)
=⋂𝜙(𝑥)∈𝑉𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥(6.2.114)
=𝒪︀𝑋(𝜙−1(𝑉))(6.2.73)

By (6.2.54) dim𝑉=dim𝑌=1 and therefore dim𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉)=1 (6.1.50). By (3.35.61) 𝐵 is a Dedekind domain and a finite 𝐴-module with quotient field 𝑘(𝑋).

Let 𝑈≔𝜙−1(𝑉) and observe that as 𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥 is integrally closed

𝐵⊂𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥⟺𝜙⋆(𝐴)⊂𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥⟺𝐴⊂𝒪︀𝑌,𝜙(𝑥)⟺𝜙(𝑥)∈𝑉⟺𝑥∈𝑈

where we have used the fact 𝑉 is affine (6.2.114). This shows that there is a bijection between 𝑈0 and the valuation rings of 𝑘(𝑋) containing 𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈). It remains to show that 𝑈 is affine.

Let 𝑍 denote an integral affine curve with coordinate ring (isomorphic to) 𝐵=𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈). By the Affine Mapping Property (6.2.22) (applicable to 𝑈 without yet knowing it is affine, since only 𝑍 needs to be) there is a corresponding regular morphism

𝜓:𝑈→𝑍

such that 𝜓𝑍♯:𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍)→𝒪︀𝑈(𝑈) is an isomorphism. Consider the commutative

as 𝑘(𝑍) is the field of fractions of 𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍) and similarly for 𝒪︀𝑈(𝑈) (6.2.15), we see that 𝜓⋆ is an isomorphism. In light of the correspondence of valuation rings to points we see that 𝜓0:𝑈0→𝑍0 is a bijection. As these have the cofinite topology (6.2.113) then 𝜓0 is necessarily a homeomorphism.

For 𝑔∈𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍) we have a commutative diagram

where the bottom isomorphisms follow from (6.2.27). This shows that 𝜓𝐷(𝑔)♯ is an isomorphism, and in particular (as the 𝐷(𝑔) form a basis of 𝑍) that 𝜓 is continuous. We claim that the morphism of stalks

𝜓𝑥:𝒪︀𝑍,𝜓(𝑥)→𝒪︀𝑈,𝑥

is an isomorphism for all 𝑥∈𝑈. Suppose we have (𝑊,𝜎)∈𝒪︀𝑈,𝑥 and let 𝑔∈𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍) be such that 𝜓(𝑥)∈𝐷(𝑔)⊂𝜓(𝑊) (6.1.15). Then as 𝜓𝐷(𝑔)♯ is an isomorphism there exists 𝜏∈𝒪︀𝑍(𝐷(𝑔)) such that 𝜓♯(𝜏)=𝜎|𝜓−1(𝐷(𝑔)) which has the required image in 𝒪︀𝑈,𝑥. Similarly suppose that (𝑇,𝜏)∈𝒪︀𝑍,𝜓(𝑥) maps to zero. Then there exists some neighbourhood 𝑥∈𝑊⊂𝜓−1(𝑇) such that 𝜓♯(𝜏)|𝑊=0. We may choose 𝑔∈𝒪︀𝑍(𝑍) such that 𝐷(𝑔)⊂𝜓(𝑊). Then 0=𝜓♯(𝜏)|𝜓−1(𝐷(𝑔))=𝜓♯(𝜏|𝐷(𝑔)) whence 𝜏|𝐷(𝑔)=0 which shows that (𝑇,𝜏) is zero.

By (6.2.50) (applied to 𝑈 and 𝑍), together with 𝜓0 already bijective and each stalk map 𝜓𝑥 already an isomorphism, 𝜓 is bijective. As 𝜓 is a continuous bijection inducing the homeomorphism 𝜓0 on Kolmogorov quotients, (4.1.38) shows 𝜓 is a homeomorphism.

As 𝜓♯ is an isomorphism on a basis of open sets, it is an isomorphism of sheaves. Therefore 𝑈 is isomorphic to 𝑍 and affine as required. ∎

Definition 6.2.120 (Order of Zero / Poles)

Let 𝑋 be a regular algebraic curve. For every point 𝑥∈𝑋 there is a well-defined and unique discrete valuation

𝑣𝑥:𝑘(𝑋)⋆→ℤ

because 𝒪︀𝑥,𝑋 is a discrete valuation ring of 𝑘(𝑋) (6.2.114). For 𝑟 a positive integer we say that 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋)⋆ has a zero (resp. pole) of order 𝑟 at 𝑥 if 𝑣𝑥(𝑓)=𝑟 (resp. 𝑣𝑥(𝑓)=−𝑟).

As before define the principal divisor

(𝑓)=∑𝑥∈𝑋0𝑣𝑥(𝑓)𝑥

on the free abelian group indexed by 𝑋0.

Definition 6.2.121

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism of regular curves and 𝜙⋆:𝑘(𝑌)↪︎𝑘(𝑋) the correspond morphism of fields. Recall that for 𝑥∈𝑋 that 𝜙⋆ restricts to a local homomorphism

𝒪︀𝑌,𝜙(𝑥)→𝒪︀𝑋,𝑥

Therefore for 𝑥∈𝑋 we may define the ramification index at 𝑥 as follows

𝑒𝑥≔𝑣𝑥(𝜙⋆(𝑡))≥1

where 𝑡 is a uniformiser for the discrete valuation ring 𝒪︀𝑌,𝜙(𝑥). Similarly the residue degree is given by the degree of the field extension

𝑓𝑥≔[𝑘(𝔪𝑋,𝑥):𝜙⋆𝑘(𝔪𝑌,𝜙(𝑥))]

Observe that if 𝑥 and 𝑥′ are topologically indistinguishable (equivalently Galois conjugate, or equal in 𝑋0) then 𝑒𝑥=𝑒𝑥′ and 𝑓𝑥=𝑓𝑥′.

Note when 𝑘 is algebraically closed then 𝑓𝑥=1 since 𝑘(𝑥),𝑘(𝑦) are finite and therefore trivial extensions of 𝑘.

Proposition 6.2.122 (Ramification Formula)

Let 𝜙:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism of regular curves which is finite (e.g. 𝑋 and 𝑌 are complete (6.2.119)). For 𝑦∈𝑌 then

deg(𝜙)=∑𝑥0∈𝜙0−1({𝑦0})𝑒𝑥𝑓𝑥

Proof. Let 𝑉 be an affine neighbourhood of 𝑦, and define 𝑈=𝜙−1(𝑉). Then by assumption 𝑈 is affine and 𝜙♯:𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉)→𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈) is finite (and integral (3.24.4)).

Define 𝐿≔𝑘(𝑌), 𝐵≔𝒪︀𝑌(𝑉), 𝐾≔𝜙⋆(𝑘(𝑋)) and 𝐴≔𝜙⋆(𝒪︀𝑋(𝑈)), where 𝜙⋆:𝑘(𝑋)↪︎𝑘(𝑌) is the canonical embedding

Then by (6.2.15) 𝐿 is the quotient field of 𝐵, and 𝐾 is the quotient field of 𝐴. By (6.2.101) (6.2.54) both 𝐵 and 𝐴 are Dedekind domains. 𝐵 is finite and integral over 𝐴, and therefore 𝐵 is the integral closure of 𝐴, being integrally closed. Therefore we are in the situation of (3.32.10).

By (6.2.21) there is a bijection between the maximal ideals of 𝐵 (resp. 𝐴) and the points of 𝑈0 (resp. 𝑉0). And by (…) 𝜙0(𝑥0)=𝑦0⟺𝔐𝑈,𝑥∩𝐴=𝔐𝑉,𝑦.

By (3.32.15) the notion of ramification index and residue degree coincide with the same notions for Dedekind domains. Therefore the result follows from the corresponding result for finite morphisms of Dedekind domains (3.32.16). ∎

Proposition 6.2.123 (Degree of Principal Divisor is Zero)

Let 𝑋 be a complete regular curve and 𝑓∈𝑘(𝑋) a non-constant rational function, then

deg((𝑓))=0

i.e. the degree of a principal divisor is zero.

Proof. By (6.2.118) 𝑓 corresponds to a non-constant and therefore surjective regular morphism 𝜙𝑓:𝑋→ℙ𝑘1→∼𝔸𝑘1∪{∞}. From the construction we see that 𝑣𝑥(𝑓)>0 if and only if 𝜙𝑓(𝑥)=0 and 𝑣𝑥(𝑓)<0 if and only if 𝜙𝑓(𝑥)=∞. Therefore by definition

(𝑓)=∑𝑥0∈𝑋0𝜙(𝑥0)=0𝑣𝑥0(𝑓)𝑥0+∑𝑥0∈𝑋0𝜙(𝑥0)=∞𝑣𝑥0(𝑓)𝑥0

We have canonical isomorphism 𝒪︀ℙ𝑘1,0→∼𝑘[𝑋](𝑋) and when 𝜙𝑓(𝑥)=0 the corresponding morphisms of stalks is given by 𝑋→𝑓𝑥, therefore the ramification index is 𝑒𝑥=𝑣𝑥(𝑓). Similarly when 𝜙𝑓(𝑥)=∞ we have 𝑒𝑥=𝑣𝑥(𝑓−1)=−𝑣𝑥(𝑓). It’s evident that 𝑘(𝔪ℙ𝑘1,0)=𝑘, whence 𝑓𝑥0=[𝑘(𝑥0):𝑘]. Therefore by definition of degree

deg((𝑓))=∑𝑥0∈𝑋0𝜙(𝑥0)=0𝑒𝑥0𝑓𝑥0−∑𝑥0∈𝑋0𝜙(𝑥0)=∞𝑒𝑥0𝑓𝑥0

As 𝑋 is complete, and so is ℙ𝑘1 (6.2.95) then 𝜙𝑓 is finite by (6.2.119) and we are done by (6.2.122) since both sums are equal to deg(𝜙𝑓). ∎
